lessons.title: Ohm's law, Kirchhoff's laws and resistor networks

scenes.text: An electrician finds one lamp in a string dark and wonders if the others are series or parallel.
KCL and KVL tell exactly what current flows where.

steps.title: Basic laws
steps.body:
Ohm: V = IR; power P = VI = I²R = V²/R. Resistance R = ρL/A, R_T = R₀(1 + α₀T).
**KCL:** Σ currents entering a node = 0 (charge conservation).
**KVL:** Σ voltages around a closed loop = 0 (energy conservation).
Series R_eq = ΣR (same current, voltage divides: Vₖ = V Rₖ/R_eq). Parallel 1/R_eq = Σ1/R (same voltage, current divides: I₁ = I R₂/(R₁ + R₂)).

steps.title: Star–delta transformation
steps.body:
Δ → Y: R_a = R_ab R_ca/(R_ab + R_bc + R_ca) (product of adjacent / sum).
Y → Δ: R_ab = R_a + R_b + R_aR_b/R_c (sum of two + their product / third).
Equal resistors: R_Y = R_Δ/3.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** 4 Ω in series with (6 ∥ 3) across 12 V: 6 ∥ 3 = 2 Ω ⇒ R = 6 Ω, I = 2 A; current in 6 Ω = 2 × 3/9 = 0.667 A.

**Example 2.** Δ of 30 Ω each → Y of 10 Ω each.

**Example 3.** A 100 W, 230 V lamp: R = V²/P = 529 Ω; I = 0.435 A.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Inconsistent sign conventions in KVL (choose a direction and stick to it).
- Adding parallel resistances directly.
- Using star–delta formulas the wrong way round.

activity.prompt: Three resistors 2 Ω, 3 Ω, 6 Ω in parallel. Equivalent resistance (Ω)?

quiz.q: KCL is based on conservation of
quiz.why: Kirchhoff's current law says the algebraic sum of currents at a node is zero, which expresses conservation of charge.
Two equal resistors in parallel give half: 10/2 = 5 Ω.

quiz.q: Δ of 9 Ω each converts to Y of
quiz.why: A delta of equal resistors R converts to a star of R/3 each: 9/3 = 3 Ω.

quiz.q: In series, the quantity common to all elements is
quiz.why: In a series circuit there is only one path, so the same current flows through every element.

lessons.title: Mesh and nodal analysis

scenes.text: An engineer must find the current in a bridge resistor of a sensor circuit.
Mesh or nodal analysis gives a set of linear equations — solved systematically.

steps.title: Methods
steps.body:
**Mesh (loop) analysis:** assign clockwise mesh currents; write KVL for each mesh; shared resistors carry the difference of mesh currents. Number of equations = number of independent meshes.
**Nodal analysis:** choose a reference node; write KCL at other nodes with currents (V_node − V_other)/R. Number of equations = nodes − 1.
Supermesh (current source between meshes) and supernode (voltage source between nodes) handle sources.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1 (mesh).** 10 V source, R₁ = 2 Ω in mesh 1, shared R₂ = 4 Ω, R₃ = 6 Ω in mesh 2 (no source).
Mesh 1: 10 = 6I₁ − 4I₂. Mesh 2: 0 = −4I₁ + 10I₂ ⇒ I₁ = 2.5I₂ ⇒ 10 = 15I₂ − 4I₂ = 11I₂ ⇒ I₂ = 0.909 A, I₁ = 2.273 A. Current in R₂ = 1.364 A.

**Example 2 (nodal).** Node V connected to 12 V through 2 Ω, to ground through 4 Ω and 4 Ω: (V − 12)/2 + V/4 + V/4 = 0 ⇒ V(1/2 + 1/2) = 6 ⇒ V = 6 V.

steps.title: Which method?
steps.body: Fewer meshes than nodes? Use mesh. Many parallel branches and current sources? Use nodal. Both give the same answer — pick the one with fewer equations.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting that a shared resistor's voltage uses (I₁ − I₂).
- Wrong reference node signs.
- Not converting a current source into a supermesh constraint.

activity.prompt: Nodal: node V linked to 10 V via 5 Ω and to ground via 5 Ω. V = ?

quiz.q: Equations in nodal analysis with n nodes
quiz.why: With n nodes, one is chosen as the reference, leaving n − 1 independent nodal equations.
Mesh analysis applies Kirchhoff's voltage law around each independent mesh (loop).
A supernode is formed when a voltage source connects two non-reference nodes, so that the two nodes are treated together.
options: a current source is in a mesh
a voltage source joins two non-reference nodes

quiz.q: Current in a shared resistor (meshes clockwise)
quiz.why: If meshes are both taken clockwise, a resistor shared by two meshes has mesh currents in opposite directions, so the current through it is I₁ − I₂.
Mesh analysis applies only to planar circuits (those that can be drawn without crossing wires).

lessons.title: Superposition, Thevenin and Norton theorems

scenes.text: A designer tests 10 different loads on the same complicated circuit.
Thevenin reduces the circuit to one source and one resistor — each load is then a one-line calculation.

steps.title: Superposition
steps.body: In a linear circuit with several sources, the response = sum of responses to each source acting alone (other voltage sources shorted, current sources opened). Not valid for power directly (power is non-linear).

steps.title: Thevenin and Norton
steps.body:
Any linear two-terminal network = V_th in series with R_th (Thevenin) or I_N in parallel with R_N (Norton).
V_th = open-circuit voltage; I_N = short-circuit current; R_th = R_N = resistance seen with independent sources deactivated = V_th/I_N.
Load current I_L = V_th/(R_th + R_L).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1 (Thevenin).** 24 V source with 4 Ω series, then 12 Ω across terminals A–B. V_th = 24 × 12/16 = 18 V; R_th = 4 ∥ 12 = 3 Ω. For R_L = 6 Ω: I_L = 18/9 = 2 A.

**Example 2 (Norton).** Same: I_N = 24/4 = 6 A (12 Ω shorted); R_N = 3 Ω; check V_th = 6 × 3 = 18 V ✔

**Example 3 (superposition).** 10 V source with 5 Ω, a 2 A current source, common 5 Ω load: from V alone I = 1 A; from I alone (V shorted) I = 1 A in load ⇒ total 2 A.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Opening voltage sources (they must be shorted) when finding R_th.
- Including the load resistor when finding V_th.
- Superposing powers.

activity.prompt: Finding the Thevenin equivalent
items: Remove the load from terminals A–B
Find the open-circuit voltage V_th
Deactivate independent sources (V short, I open)
Find R_th seen from A–B
Reconnect load: I_L = V_th/(R_th + R_L)

quiz.why: To find R_th, independent voltage sources are short-circuited, because an ideal voltage source has zero internal resistance.
The Norton current is the current through a short circuit placed across the output terminals.
R_th = V_th/I_N, the open-circuit voltage divided by the short-circuit current.

quiz.q: Superposition cannot be used to find
quiz.why: Superposition holds for linear quantities (current and voltage), but power is proportional to the square, so it cannot be added directly.
Thevenin's theorem applies to linear networks, where superposition and Ohm's law hold.

lessons.title: Maximum power transfer and source transformation

story.title: Getting the most from a solar panel

scenes.text: A small solar charger delivers the most power only into the right load.
Maximum power transfer: match the load to the source's internal resistance.

steps.title: Maximum power transfer
steps.body: Power to R_L is maximum when R_L = R_th: P_max = V_th²/(4R_th). Efficiency at that point is only 50% — used in communication/signal circuits, not in power distribution.

steps.title: Source transformation
steps.body: A voltage source V with series R ⇔ current source V/R with parallel R. Useful for combining sources and simplifying before mesh/nodal analysis.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** V_th = 18 V, R_th = 3 Ω ⇒ R_L = 3 Ω, P_max = 324/12 = 27 W.

**Example 2.** At R_L = 6 Ω: I = 2 A, P = 24 W (less than 27 W).

**Example 3.** 12 V with 4 Ω ⇔ 3 A source with 4 Ω in parallel.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking maximum power means maximum efficiency.
- Using P_max = V²/R_th (missing the factor 4).
- Forgetting to keep the same resistor in source transformation.

activity.label: Load resistance for a source with V_th = 12 V, R_th = 4 Ω

bands.text: Below R_th: high current, less than maximum power, poor efficiency.
Near R_L = R_th: maximum power (9 W) at 50% efficiency.
Above R_th: less power but higher efficiency.

quiz.why: Maximum power is transferred to a load when R_L = R_th.
At R_L = R_th, the current is V_th/(2R_th), so P_max = (V_th/2R_th)² R_th = V_th²/(4R_th).
At matching, the same power is lost in R_th as is delivered to the load, so the efficiency is 50%.
Source transformation: a voltage source V with series R is equivalent to a current source V/R = 10/2 = 5 A in parallel with R = 2 Ω.

quiz.q: Power grids avoid matched loads because
quiz.why: Power systems avoid matched loads because half the power would be wasted in the source and lines (efficiency only 50%).

lessons.title: Sinusoids, RMS values and phasors

scenes.text: The socket says 230 V, but the voltage actually swings ±325 V fifty times a second.
230 V is the RMS value — the DC voltage that heats a resistor equally.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
v = V_m sin(ωt + φ), ω = 2πf. RMS V = V_m/√2 (sinusoid). Average (half cycle) V_av = 2V_m/π = 0.637V_m.
Form factor = RMS/average = 1.11; peak (crest) factor = V_m/RMS = 1.414.
Phasor: rotating vector of length RMS at angle φ; V = V∠φ = V(cos φ + j sin φ).

steps.title: Complex arithmetic
steps.body: Add/subtract in rectangular form, multiply/divide in polar form. j = √(−1) means a 90° rotation.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding RMS magnitudes of phasors with different angles.
- Using degrees in ωt computations that need radians.
- Using RMS formulas for non-sinusoidal waves.

activity.prompt: Peak value of 230 V RMS sinusoid (V)?

quiz.why: The RMS value of a sinusoid is V_m/√2 ≈ 0.707 V_m.
Form factor = RMS/average. For a sine wave, (Vm/√2)/(2Vm/π) = π/(2√2) ≈ 0.707/0.637 ≈ 1.11.
In polar form, multiply the magnitudes and add the angles.

sources: Standard Basic Electrical Engineering syllabus (first year)

lessons.title: R, L, C elements and series circuits

scenes.text: An old fan regulator used an inductor (choke) to drop voltage with little heat loss.
Inductive reactance opposes AC without dissipating power.

steps.title: Elements
steps.body:
- R: V and I in phase; Z = R.
- L: current lags voltage by 90°; X_L = ωL = 2πfL; Z = jX_L.
- C: current leads voltage by 90°; X_C = 1/(ωC); Z = −jX_C.
Series RLC: Z = R + j(X_L − X_C), |Z| = √(R² + (X_L − X_C)²), φ = tan⁻¹[(X_L − X_C)/R]. Inductive if X_L > X_C (lagging), capacitive if X_C > X_L (leading).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Series R = 30 Ω, L = 0.127 H, 230 V, 50 Hz: X_L = 39.9 ≈ 40 Ω; Z = 50 Ω; I = 4.6 A; φ = 53.1° lag; pf = 0.6.

**Example 2.** Series R = 10 Ω, X_L = 20 Ω, X_C = 10 Ω, V = 100 V: Z = 10 + j10 = 14.14∠45° ⇒ I = 7.07∠−45° A; V_R = 70.7, V_L = 141.4, V_C = 70.7 V (individual voltages can exceed supply).

steps.title: Impedance triangle
steps.body: R (base), X (height), Z (hypotenuse); cos φ = R/Z. The voltage triangle V_R, V_X, V is the same shape scaled by I.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding V_R + V_L + V_C arithmetically.
- Forgetting X_C decreases with frequency.
- Using C in µF without converting to F.

activity.prompt: X_C of a 100 µF capacitor at 50 Hz (Ω)?

quiz.why: In a pure inductor the current lags the voltage by 90°.
pf = cos φ = R/|Z| = 3/5 = 0.6, lagging as the circuit is inductive.
X_C = 1/(2πfC) is inversely proportional to frequency, so doubling f halves X_C.

sources: Standard Basic Electrical Engineering syllabus (first year)

lessons.title: Power, power factor and its improvement

scenes.text: A factory pays a penalty because its power factor is 0.7.
Installing capacitor banks raises pf and cuts the bill.

steps.title: Power relations
steps.body:
Active P = VI cos φ (W); reactive Q = VI sin φ (VAR); apparent S = VI (VA). S² = P² + Q². Complex power S = VI* = P + jQ.
Power factor = cos φ = P/S. Low pf ⇒ more current for the same power ⇒ larger I²R losses, bigger cables, voltage drops.

steps.title: Improving power factor
steps.body: Add a shunt capacitor supplying Q_C = P(tan φ₁ − tan φ₂). C = Q_C/(ωV²). Synchronous condensers and phase advancers are alternatives in large installations.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling VA 'watts'.
- Using sin φ in place of cos φ for active power.
- Trying to 'improve' pf above 1 or overcorrecting to leading.

activity.prompt: Load: V = 230 V, I = 10 A, pf = 0.8. Active power in W?

quiz.why: Reactive power is measured in VAR (volt-ampere reactive).
In the power triangle S² = P² + Q².
Capacitors supply leading reactive power, so they improve the power factor of inductive (lagging) loads.
A low power factor means a larger current for the same real power, which raises I²R losses and cable and equipment size.
For a pure resistor the voltage and current are in phase, φ = 0, so pf = cos 0 = 1.

sources: Standard Basic Electrical Engineering syllabus (first year)

lessons.title: Parallel circuits and resonance

scenes.text: Turning a radio dial changes a capacitor until the circuit resonates with one station.
At resonance the LC circuit picks one frequency and rejects others.

steps.title: Series resonance
steps.body: X_L = X_C ⇒ f₀ = 1/(2π√(LC)). Z = R (minimum), I = V/R (maximum), pf = 1. Quality factor Q = ω₀L/R = (1/R)√(L/C); bandwidth BW = f₀/Q; voltage across L or C = Q × V (voltage magnification).

steps.title: Parallel circuits and resonance
steps.body: Use admittance Y = 1/Z = G + jB; branch currents add as phasors. Parallel (tank) circuit of coil (R, L) with C: f₀ = (1/2π)√(1/LC − R²/L²); dynamic impedance Z_D = L/(CR) (maximum), current minimum — current magnification Q.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Assuming the parallel resonant frequency equals 1/(2π√LC) when R is significant.
- Thinking resonance means zero current (that is the parallel case with high Z, not zero).
- Forgetting the high component voltages in series resonance — insulation must handle them.

activity.prompt: Series vs parallel resonance

quiz.why: At resonance X_L = X_C, so ωL = 1/(ωC), giving f₀ = 1/(2π√(LC)).
At series resonance X_L = X_C cancel, so Z = R and the pf is unity (1).
Bandwidth = f₀/Q = 1 MHz/50 = 20 kHz.
Parallel resonance is called anti-resonance, as the impedance is maximum and the circuit rejects the resonant frequency (a rejector circuit).
Admittance is the reciprocal of impedance: Y = 1/Z.

questions.why: In an ideal capacitor the current leads the voltage by 90°.

questions.why: The average value over a half cycle is 2I_m/π = 2 × 10/π = 6.37 A.

questions.q: Z of R = 6 Ω, X_C = 8 Ω series
questions.why: Z = R − jX_C = 6 − j8, so |Z| = 10 Ω and the angle is −tan⁻¹(8/6) = −53.1° (current leads).

questions.q: Q of a 5 kW, 0.8 pf load
Assertion (A): In series resonance, voltage across L can exceed the supply voltage.  Reason (R): Voltage across L = Q × V at resonance.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: Both true: at resonance the voltage across L equals Q × V, which is greater than the supply voltage when Q > 1. This is voltage magnification.

questions.q: f₀ for L = 1 mH, C = 1 µF
Current in R = 20 Ω, X_L = 15 Ω series on 250 V
Capacitor kVAR to raise 20 kW from 0.8 to 1.0 pf
questions.why: Initial Q = P tan φ₁ = 20 tan 36.87° = 15 kVAR. For unity pf the capacitor must supply all of it, 15 kVAR.

questions.q: Case: A 230 V, 50 Hz pump draws 8 A at 0.75 lagging. Capacitance to correct to unity
questions.why: Reactive power now Q = VI sinφ = 230·8·0.661 ≈ 1217 VAR. To reach unity pf the capacitor must supply all of it: C = Q/(ωV²) = 1217/(314·52900) ≈ 73 µF. The other values are off by factors of 10.

questions.q: Two parallel branches 10∠0° A and 10∠−90° A. Total current
questions.why: Add the currents as phasors, not as plain numbers. 10∠0° = 10 + j0 and 10∠−90° = 0 − j10, so the sum is 10 − j10, which has magnitude √(100+100) = 14.14 A and angle −45°. Adding 10 + 10 = 20 A would wrongly assume the currents are in phase.

questions.q: Series RLC: R 10, L 0.2 H, C 50 µF. Q-factor
questions.why: For a series RLC circuit Q = (1/R)√(L/C) = (1/10)√(0.2/50×10⁻⁶) = 0.1 × √4000 ≈ 0.1 × 63.2 = 6.32. A decimal slip gives the tempting wrong values 0.632 or 63.2.

questions.q: Dynamic impedance of tank with L = 1 mH, C = 0.1 µF, R = 10 Ω
questions.why: At resonance a parallel tank has dynamic impedance Z = L/(CR) = 10⁻³/(0.1×10⁻⁶ × 10) = 10⁻³/10⁻⁶ = 1000 Ω = 1 kΩ. It is far larger than R because the L and C branch currents circulate inside the tank.

questions.q: Instantaneous power in an AC resistor oscillates at
questions.why: With v = Vm sin ωt and i = Im sin ωt, p = vi = VmIm sin²ωt = (VmIm/2)(1 − cos 2ωt). The cos 2ωt term makes power oscillate at twice the supply frequency, always staying ≥ 0 for a resistor.

lessons.title: Three-phase supply: star and delta

scenes.text: A workshop's lathe motor needs a three-phase connection; homes usually get one phase.
Three phases 120° apart give constant power and smaller conductors.

steps.title: Generation and sequence
steps.body: Three windings 120° apart produce v_R = V_m sin ωt, v_Y = V_m sin(ωt − 120°), v_B = V_m sin(ωt − 240°). Phase sequence RYB. Balanced system: equal magnitudes, 120° apart; phasor sum = 0.

steps.title: Star and delta relations (balanced)
steps.body:
**Star (Y):** V_L = √3 V_ph, I_L = I_ph; line voltage leads phase voltage by 30°. Neutral available (4-wire: 400 V line, 230 V phase in India).
**Delta (Δ):** V_L = V_ph, I_L = √3 I_ph; line current lags phase current by 30°.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** 400 V star supply: V_ph = 400/√3 = 231 V.

**Example 2.** Balanced delta load, each phase 10 + j10 Ω, on 400 V: Z_ph = 14.14 Ω; I_ph = 28.3 A; I_L = 49 A.

**Example 3.** Same impedances in star on 400 V: V_ph = 231 V, I_ph = I_L = 16.3 A — one-third of the delta line current.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying √3 to current in a star connection.
- Using line voltage as phase voltage in star loads.
- Forgetting the 30° shift between line and phase quantities.

activity.prompt: Star or delta relation?

quiz.why: In a balanced three-phase supply the three voltages are equal in size and each is displaced by 120° (one third of a 360° cycle) from the next. 90° and 60° are not used for this.

quiz.q: Line voltage in star with V_ph = 230 V
quiz.why: In a star connection the line voltage is √3 times the phase voltage: 230 × 1.732 ≈ 398–400 V. This is why a 230 V phase gives the familiar 400 V line supply.
In a delta connection each line current is the phasor difference of two phase currents, which gives a magnitude of √3 × phase current for a balanced load. Line and phase voltages are equal in delta.
Balanced phase voltages have equal magnitude and are 120° apart. Their phasors form a closed triangle, so V + V∠−120° + V∠120° = 0.

quiz.q: Same Z in star draws ___ the line current of delta
quiz.why: For the same Z per phase, delta puts the full line voltage across each Z and gets I_L = √3·V_L/Z. Star puts only V_L/√3 across it and gets I_L = V_L/(√3Z). The ratio is 1/3, so star draws one-third of the line current.

sources: Standard Basic Electrical Engineering syllabus (first year)

lessons.title: Three-phase power and the two-wattmeter method

scenes.text: An engineer measures a 3-phase motor with only two wattmeters.
Their sum gives total power; their difference reveals the power factor.

steps.title: Power
steps.body: P = √3 V_L I_L cos φ = 3V_ph I_ph cos φ (φ = angle of the phase impedance). Q = √3 V_L I_L sin φ; S = √3 V_L I_L. Total instantaneous power in a balanced system is constant — smoother motor torque.

steps.title: Two-wattmeter method
steps.body:
Current coils in two lines, pressure coils between each of those lines and the third. Works for any 3-wire load (balanced or not). For balanced loads:
W₁ = V_L I_L cos(30° − φ), W₂ = V_L I_L cos(30° + φ).
P = W₁ + W₂; tan φ = √3(W₁ − W₂)/(W₁ + W₂).
pf = 0.5 ⇒ W₂ = 0; pf < 0.5 ⇒ W₂ reads negative (reverse its connection).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using phase voltage with line current in P = √3 V I cos φ.
- Ignoring the sign of a reversed wattmeter.
- Thinking two wattmeters fail for unbalanced loads (they work for any 3-wire load).

activity.prompt: Two-wattmeter: W₁ = 3 kW, W₂ = 3 kW. Power factor?

quiz.why: Total balanced three-phase power is P = 3V_ph I_ph cos φ. Since V_ph I_ph = V_L I_L/√3 for both star and delta, P = √3 V_L I_L cos φ. The cos φ factor is needed for real power.
In the two-wattmeter method W₁ = V_L I_L cos(30° − φ) and W₂ = V_L I_L cos(30° + φ). W₂ = 0 means 30° + φ = 90°, so φ = 60° and pf = cos 60° = 0.5.
W₂ = V_L I_L cos(30° + φ) goes negative when 30° + φ > 90°, which means φ > 60°. Since cos 60° = 0.5, the power factor must be below 0.5.
By Blondel's theorem, n wires need n − 1 wattmeters. So two wattmeters measure the total power in any three-wire system, balanced or not. A four-wire load needs three.
The two wattmeter readings add algebraically to the total instantaneous power, so P = W₁ + W₂. Their difference only relates to reactive power, as √3(W₁ − W₂) = Q.

lessons.title: Domestic wiring, earthing and protection

scenes.text: Riya feels a tingle touching her washing machine.
Faulty earthing! An RCCB would have tripped and protected her.

steps.title: Wiring and components
steps.body: Indian domestic supply: single-phase 230 V, 50 Hz (phase, neutral, earth). Distribution board with main switch, MCBs per circuit, RCCB/ELCB. Wiring types: conduit (concealed/surface), casing–capping (older), cleat (temporary). Colour codes (IS): red/brown phase, black/blue neutral, green/green-yellow earth. Lighting circuits ~6 A, power sockets 16 A.

steps.title: Protective devices and earthing
steps.body:
- **Fuse:** melts on overcurrent; cheap, single use.
- **MCB:** thermal (overload) + magnetic (short circuit) trip; resettable.
- **RCCB/ELCB:** trips on leakage (phase–neutral current imbalance), typically 30 mA for personal protection.
- **Earthing:** connects metal bodies to earth so fault current trips the protection and touch voltage stays low. Types: plate earthing, pipe earthing; lower earth resistance is better (wet soil, salt and charcoal layers).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** A 2 kW geyser on 230 V: I = 8.7 A ⇒ use a 16 A circuit and suitable cable.

**Example 2.** Why RCCB for bathrooms? A person touching a live part leaks current to earth; at 30 mA the RCCB trips in tens of milliseconds, before ventricular fibrillation is likely.

steps.title: Safety rules (non-negotiable)
steps.body:
- Switch off and lock out the MCB before any work; verify dead with a tester.
- Never bypass a fuse with thicker wire or defeat an RCCB.
- Don't handle appliances with wet hands; use insulated tools and rubber mats.
- For electric shock: switch off supply first, don't touch the victim directly, call 112, start CPR if trained.
- This is general education — wiring work should be done by a licensed electrician.

activity.prompt: Home electrical safety check
items: Main switch and MCBs labelled
RCCB (30 mA) installed and test button works
All metal appliances have three-pin plugs with earth
No overloaded multi-plug adapters
Earth pit/resistance checked by an electrician

quiz.why: An RCCB compares the current going out with the current returning. If some leaks to earth, the two differ, and the imbalance trips the device. It does not respond to power factor, frequency or overvoltage.
An MCB uses a thermal element for slow overloads and a magnetic element for sudden short circuits. It does not detect small earth leakage, which is the RCCB's job.
Under the Indian standard the earth conductor is green or green-yellow. Black, red and blue are used for live or neutral conductors, so mixing them up is dangerous.
Personal-protection RCCBs are rated at about 30 mA, because currents above that can be dangerous to the body. Ratings of 300 mA or more are for fire protection, and 1 mA would trip nuisance-often.

quiz.q: First action when someone gets a shock
quiz.why: First switch off the supply, so the person is no longer in the circuit and the rescuer is safe. Touching them while the current flows can shock you too. Water also conducts electricity and makes it worse.

lessons.title: Energy, tariffs and batteries in installations

scenes.text: A family's bill shows 300 units in a month.
One 'unit' is 1 kWh. Knowing that, they cut the bill by tracking their big loads.

steps.title: Energy and billing
steps.body: Energy (kWh) = power (kW) × time (h). 1 unit = 1 kWh = 3.6 MJ. Tariffs often use slabs (rate rises with consumption) plus fixed/demand charges; industries also pay for kVA demand and low pf penalties. Check your local electricity board's current rates — they vary by state and change over time.

steps.title: Backup and storage
steps.body: UPS/inverter with lead–acid or Li-ion batteries. Battery energy (Wh) = V × Ah. Backup time ≈ (V × Ah × depth-of-discharge × inverter efficiency)/load W. Cables sized by current and voltage drop; batteries need ventilation (lead–acid releases hydrogen during charging).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Monthly energy: 5 LED lamps × 10 W × 6 h × 30 days = 9 kWh; fridge 150 W average × 24 h × 30 = 108 kWh; total 117 units.

**Example 2.** 12 V 150 Ah battery, 50% DoD, 85% inverter, 200 W load: backup = 12 × 150 × 0.5 × 0.85/200 ≈ 3.8 h.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing kW (power) with kWh (energy).
- Ignoring depth-of-discharge and inverter losses in backup estimates.
- Using a fixed per-unit rate for a slab tariff.

activity.prompt: A 1.5 kW AC runs 8 h/day for 30 days. Units consumed?

quiz.why: The billing 'unit' of electricity is one kilowatt-hour (1 kWh), the energy used by 1 kW running for 1 hour. kW is a rate of power, and J and W are far smaller.
1 kWh = 1000 W × 3600 s = 3.6 × 10⁶ J = 3.6 MJ. Many people mistake it for 3600 J or 36 MJ by dropping or adding zeros.
Energy = V × Ah = 12 × 100 = 1200 Wh = 1.2 kWh. Volts times amp-hours gives watt-hours, then divide by 1000 for kWh.

quiz.q: Industrial consumers may be penalised for
quiz.why: Low power factor means more current for the same real power, which causes extra losses in the supply network. Tariffs therefore penalise industrial consumers with low pf and reward high pf.
Charging lead–acid batteries gives off hydrogen, which is explosive in the right mixture. Battery rooms need ventilation to keep it from building up; sealing them or spraying water would not help.

sources: Standard Basic Electrical Engineering syllabus (first year)

questions.q: Line voltage of Indian 3-phase LV supply
questions.why: The standard three-phase low-voltage supply in India is 400 V between lines, which is √3 × 230 V. 11 kV is distribution voltage, and 110 V and 230 V are not line voltages here.

questions.q: Device that melts on overcurrent
questions.why: A fuse has a thin wire that melts when the current gets too high, which opens the circuit. An RCCB trips on leakage and does not melt, and a capacitor or relay coil does not do this.

questions.q: Phase displacement in 3-phase
questions.why: The three phases of a balanced supply are displaced by 120° (360°/3) from each other. 90°, 180° and 60° are not the phase displacement in a three-phase system.

questions.q: Star: V_ph = 230 V ⇒ V_L
questions.why: In star V_L = √3·V_ph = 1.732 × 230 ≈ 398 V. 690 V would be 3 × 230 and 133 V would be 230/√3, both the wrong direction or factor.

questions.q: Delta load I_ph = 10 A ⇒ I_L
questions.why: In a balanced delta, I_L = √3·I_ph = 1.732 × 10 = 17.32 A. Not 30 A, which would be 3 × 10.

questions.q: Units for a 100 W bulb for 10 h
questions.why: Energy = power × time = 100 W × 10 h = 1000 Wh = 1 kWh. Dividing by 1000 converts watt-hours to kilowatt-hours.

questions.q: Assertion (A): The two-wattmeter method measures total power in any three-phase three-wire system.  Reason (R): The sum of two wattmeter readings equals total instantaneous power by Blondel's theorem.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: A is true: n − 1 wattmeters measure total power in an n-wire system, so two do for three wires, balanced or not. R is true: Blondel's theorem gives that the two readings add up to the total power. So R is the reason for A.

questions.q: Power for 415 V, 30 A, pf 0.85 (3-phase)
questions.why: P = √3·V_L·I_L·cos φ = 1.732 × 415 × 30 × 0.85 ≈ 18 330 W ≈ 18.3 kW. Using √3 only once is needed; 31.7 kW would forget the pf.

questions.q: W₁ = 6 kW, W₂ = 2 kW ⇒ pf
Balanced star load 8 + j6 Ω per phase on 400 V: line current
questions.why: Per phase Z = √(8² + 6²) = 10 Ω. In star, phase voltage = 400/√3 ≈ 231 V, so I = 231/10 ≈ 23.1 A, and line current equals phase current.

questions.q: Total power of that star load
questions.why: Real power only dissipates in R: P = 3·I²·R = 3 × (23.1)² × 8 ≈ 12 800 W = 12.8 kW. The 6 Ω reactance uses no real power.

questions.q: Case: An RCCB trips repeatedly when the geyser is switched on. Most likely cause
questions.why: A fault leaking current from the heating element to the geyser body is an earth leakage, exactly what an RCCB senses and trips on. A high pf, low voltage or many LEDs do not cause leakage to earth.
options: leakage from the geyser element to its body

questions.q: Backup of 24 V, 100 Ah battery, 80% DoD, 90% efficient, 432 W load
questions.why: Usable energy = 24 V × 100 Ah × 0.8 × 0.9 = 1728 Wh. Time = 1728/432 = 4 h.

questions.q: Readings W₁ = W₂ in a balanced load imply
questions.why: With tan φ = √3(W₁ − W₂)/(W₁ + W₂), equal readings give tan φ = 0, so φ = 0 and the power factor is unity. A zero pf would give W₁ = −W₂, not equal readings.

questions.q: Same three resistors switched from star to delta on same supply: power becomes
questions.why: In delta each resistor sees the line voltage instead of V/√3, so phase voltage goes up by √3. Power ∝ V², so it rises by (√3)² = 3 times.

lessons.title: Magnetic circuits and induction

scenes.text: A scrap-yard crane lifts cars with an electromagnet.
Its design uses a magnetic 'Ohm's law': flux = mmf/reluctance.

steps.title: Magnetic circuit
steps.body:
mmf F = NI (ampere-turns); reluctance S = l/(μ₀μᵣA); flux Φ = F/S; B = Φ/A; H = NI/l; B = μH. Air gaps dominate reluctance since μᵣ(air) = 1.
Analogy: mmf ↔ emf, flux ↔ current, reluctance ↔ resistance. Leakage and fringing cause differences.

steps.title: Induction
steps.body:
Faraday: e = −N dΦ/dt; Lenz: induced current opposes the change. Statically induced (transformer) vs dynamically induced (e = Blv in a moving conductor). Self-inductance L = NΦ/I = N²/S; mutual M = k√(L₁L₂). Energy in an inductor ½LI².
Hysteresis loss ∝ B_m^1.6 f (Steinmetz); eddy-current loss ∝ B_m²f²t² (reduced by laminations).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Iron ring l = 0.5 m, A = 4 cm², μᵣ = 1000, N = 500, I = 1 A: S = 0.5/(4π×10⁻⁷ × 1000 × 4×10⁻⁴) = 9.95×10⁵ AT/Wb; Φ = 500/9.95×10⁵ = 0.503 mWb; B = 1.26 T.

**Example 2.** Add a 1 mm air gap: S_gap = 10⁻³/(4π×10⁻⁷ × 4×10⁻⁴) = 1.99×10⁶ — twice the iron's reluctance; flux falls to 0.168 mWb.

**Example 3.** Conductor 0.5 m long moving at 10 m/s across B = 0.8 T: e = 4 V.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Ignoring the air gap reluctance.
- Using cm² as m² (factor 10⁻⁴).
- Forgetting that laminations reduce eddy losses, not hysteresis.

activity.prompt: mmf of a 200-turn coil carrying 2.5 A (AT)?

quiz.why: Reluctance is the opposition to flux in a magnetic circuit: S = l/(μA). It is the magnetic analogue of resistance, R = l/(σA). The expression μA/l would be its inverse, permeance.
Magnetomotive force is F = NI, so its SI unit is the ampere-turn. Henry is inductance, weber is flux and tesla is flux density.
Laminations are thin insulated sheets that break up the paths for eddy currents in the core, so eddy-current loss falls. Hysteresis loss depends on the core material instead.
A conductor moving across a magnetic field has a dynamically induced emf e = Blv. ½LI² is stored energy, and N dΦ/dt is the statically induced emf in a transformer.
Energy stored in an inductor = ½LI² = ½ × 2 × 3² = 9 J. Using LI or forgetting to square the current gives wrong answers.

sources: Standard Basic Electrical Engineering syllabus (first year)

lessons.title: Single-phase transformer

scenes.text: Older phone chargers were heavy because they contained a small transformer stepping 230 V down.
Transformers change AC voltage with ~95–99% efficiency.

steps.title: Principle and construction
steps.body: Two windings on a laminated silicon-steel core linked by mutual flux; works only on AC. Core type (windings on limbs) and shell type (windings on central limb). Ideal: V₁/V₂ = N₁/N₂ = I₂/I₁ = a.

steps.title: EMF equation
steps.body: E = 4.44 f N Φ_m (RMS). On no load the primary draws a small current I₀ (magnetising + core-loss components).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** 230/12 V, 50 Hz transformer with Φ_m = 2 mWb: N₁ = 230/(4.44 × 50 × 0.002) = 518 turns; N₂ = 12/0.444 = 27 turns.

**Example 2.** 5 kVA, 2300/230 V: I₁ = 2.17 A, I₂ = 21.7 A (full load).

**Example 3.** Secondary load 46 Ω on a 10:1 step-down: impedance seen at primary = a²Z = 4600 Ω.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Connecting a transformer to DC (no changing flux ⇒ heavy current ⇒ burnout).
- Using V₁/V₂ = I₁/I₂ (it is inverse).
- Forgetting the 4.44 factor uses RMS.

activity.prompt: Transformer relations
activity.text: E = ___ f N Φm, and for an ideal transformer V₁/V₂ = N₁/N₂ = I₂/I___.

quiz.why: A transformer needs a changing flux to induce an emf in the secondary. Only AC gives continuously changing flux; DC gives constant flux and no induced emf.
V₂ = V₁ × N₂/N₁ = 2000/20 = 100 V. A 20:1 ratio steps voltage down, so the secondary voltage is smaller, not bigger.
The core is laminated so that eddy currents are limited and the iron loss is lower. It does not remove copper loss, which depends on winding resistance.
An ideal transformer keeps V₁I₁ = V₂I₂. A step-down transformer lowers voltage, so the secondary current must be greater than the primary current.
E = 4.44 f N Φm, where 4.44 comes from 2π/√2 = √2 π ≈ 4.44 (peak flux to rms emf). The other values are not this constant.

sources: Standard Basic Electrical Engineering syllabus (first year)

lessons.title: Transformer losses, efficiency and regulation

scenes.text: A colony's 250 kVA transformer runs lightly loaded at night and heavily in the evening.
It is designed for best efficiency near its typical load, not at full load.

steps.title: Losses and efficiency
steps.body:
Core (iron) loss P_i — constant (hysteresis + eddy), measured by **open-circuit test**. Copper loss P_cu = I²R — varies with load², measured by **short-circuit test**.
η = output/(output + P_i + x²P_cu,FL), x = fraction of full load. Maximum efficiency when copper loss = iron loss ⇒ x = √(P_i/P_cu,FL).
All-day efficiency = output kWh/input kWh over 24 h.

steps.title: Voltage regulation
steps.body: Regulation = (V_NL − V_FL)/V_FL × 100%. Approx: x(R_eq cos φ ± X_eq sin φ)/V × 100 (+ lagging, − leading). Can be negative at leading pf.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** 20 kVA, P_i = 300 W, P_cu,FL = 500 W, pf 0.8 at full load: output 16 kW ⇒ η = 16 000/16 800 = 95.2%.
Half load: output 8 kW, P_cu = 125 W ⇒ η = 8000/8425 = 94.96%.
Max efficiency at x = √(300/500) = 0.775 ⇒ 15.5 kVA.

**Example 2.** Percentage R = 2%, X = 4%, pf 0.8 lag: regulation ≈ 2(0.8) + 4(0.6) = 4%.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Scaling iron loss with load (it is constant).
- Forgetting x² for copper loss.
- Using the wrong sign for leading power factor in regulation.

activity.prompt: P_i = 400 W, P_cu,FL = 1600 W. Fraction of full load for maximum efficiency?

quiz.why: In the open-circuit test the rated voltage is applied with the secondary open. The no-load current is small, so copper loss is negligible, and the wattmeter reading is essentially the iron loss.
In the short-circuit test a low voltage drives rated current. The flux is small so iron loss is negligible, and the wattmeter shows the full-load copper loss.
A transformer's efficiency is highest when the variable copper loss equals the constant iron loss. Neither loss is zero there.

quiz.q: Copper loss at half load is
quiz.why: Copper loss ∝ I². At half load, (½)² = ¼ of the full-load copper loss. It is not half, since it goes with the square.
With a leading power-factor load the capacitive effect can raise the secondary voltage above its no-load value, so regulation becomes negative. Lagging loads always lower the voltage.

sources: Standard Basic Electrical Engineering syllabus (first year)

lessons.title: Rotating machines: DC, induction and synchronous

scenes.text: A ceiling fan uses a single-phase induction motor; a metro train once used DC traction motors.
Each machine converts electrical and mechanical energy using the same Faraday principle.

steps.title: DC machines
steps.body:
Generator EMF E = PΦNZ/(60A) (P poles, Φ flux/pole, N rpm, Z conductors, A parallel paths: A = 2 wave, A = P lap).
Motor: back EMF E_b = V − I_aR_a; speed N ∝ E_b/Φ; torque T ∝ ΦI_a. Types: shunt (nearly constant speed), series (high starting torque, never run unloaded), compound.

steps.title: Three-phase induction and synchronous machines
steps.body:
Three-phase currents in a distributed winding produce a rotating magnetic field at synchronous speed N_s = 120f/P rpm.
Induction motor: rotor runs slightly slower; slip s = (N_s − N)/N_s (typically 2–6% at full load); rotor frequency f_r = sf. Squirrel-cage (rugged) vs slip-ring (external resistance for starting torque).
Synchronous machine: rotor (DC excited) locks to N_s; alternators in power stations; motors need starting means. Single-phase induction motors need a starting winding/capacitor (fans, pumps).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** 4-pole, 50 Hz induction motor at 1440 rpm: N_s = 1500 rpm; s = 0.04; f_r = 2 Hz.

**Example 2.** DC shunt motor 220 V, R_a = 0.5 Ω, I_a = 20 A: E_b = 210 V.

**Example 3.** 4-pole lap DC generator, Φ = 0.02 Wb, Z = 500, N = 1200 rpm: E = 4 × 0.02 × 1200 × 500/(60 × 4) = 200 V.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Running a DC series motor without load (dangerous overspeed).
- Expecting an induction motor to run at synchronous speed (no torque at s = 0).
- Using A = 2 for lap windings.

activity.prompt: Match the machine fact

quiz.why: N_s = 120f/P = 120 × 50/6 = 1000 rpm. Using the wrong pole number gives 1500 or 750 rpm instead.
Rotor frequency is f_r = s·f = 0.05 × 50 = 2.5 Hz. A slipping rotor sees the field at only a small relative speed.
DC motor torque is proportional to flux times armature current, T ∝ ΦI_a. Speed N relates to back emf and flux, not directly to torque like this.
Ceiling fans use a single-phase induction motor with a capacitor, which gives the phase shift needed for starting and running. They are cheap and need no brushes.

sources: Standard Basic Electrical Engineering syllabus (first year)

questions.q: Unit of magnetic flux
questions.why: The SI unit of magnetic flux is the weber (Wb). Henry is for inductance, tesla for flux density and AT for mmf.

questions.q: Transformer changes
questions.why: A transformer changes the voltage level (and current) while the frequency stays the same, with nearly equal power in and out. It cannot convert DC to AC or create extra power.

questions.q: N_s of 4-pole 50 Hz
questions.why: N_s = 120f/P = 120 × 50/4 = 1500 rpm. The other options come from the wrong number of poles.

questions.q: Back EMF of 230 V motor with I_a = 10 A, R_a = 1 Ω
questions.why: Back emf E_b = V − I_aR_a = 230 − 10 × 1 = 220 V. The supply voltage is higher than the back emf by the armature drop.

questions.q: Secondary turns for 11 kV/415 V, N₁ = 2650
questions.why: N₂/N₁ = V₂/V₁, so N₂ = 2650 × 415/11000 ≈ 100 turns. The secondary has fewer turns because the voltage is stepped down.

questions.q: Iron loss of a transformer at half load if 500 W at full
questions.why: Iron loss depends on voltage and frequency, not load current. So it stays at 500 W at half load. Only copper loss falls as the square of the load.

questions.q: Assertion (A): A DC series motor must never be started without load.  Reason (R): Its speed rises dangerously because flux falls with load current.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: A is true: with no load the series field is weak, so the speed becomes dangerously high. R is also true and explains it, since N ∝ 1/Φ and flux falls when the current falls.

questions.q: Max-efficiency load for P_i = 1 kW, P_cu,FL = 4 kW, 100 kVA
questions.why: Max efficiency needs x²·P_cu,FL = P_i, so x = √(1/4) = 0.5. The load is 0.5 × 100 kVA = 50 kVA.

questions.q: Flux needed for 440 V, 50 Hz, 200 turns
Full-load η: 50 kVA, pf 1, P_i 500 W, P_cu 800 W
questions.why: Output = 50 kW at pf 1. Losses = 0.5 + 0.8 = 1.3 kW, so input = 51.3 kW, and efficiency = 50/51.3 ≈ 97.5%.

questions.q: Case: A 6-pole, 50 Hz pump motor has rotor EMF frequency 1.5 Hz. Speed
questions.why: Rotor frequency 1.5 Hz = s × 50 gives s = 0.03. N_s = 120 × 50/6 = 1000 rpm, so N = 1000(1 − 0.03) = 970 rpm.

questions.q: DC generator 6-pole wave, Φ = 0.03 Wb, Z = 400, N = 1000 rpm. E
Reluctance of 2 mm air gap, A = 10 cm²
Regulation: %R = 1.5, %X = 5, pf 0.8 leading
questions.why: Regulation ≈ %R cos φ − %X sin φ for a leading load. With cos φ = 0.8 and sin φ = 0.6: 1.5 × 0.8 − 5 × 0.6 = 1.2 − 3.0 = −1.8%. The negative value means the voltage rises.

questions.q: Primary current of 10 kVA, 230 V transformer at full load
questions.why: Full-load primary current = S/V = 10 000/230 ≈ 43.5 A. The other values come from decimal errors.

lessons.title: Formula sheet: DC and AC circuits

scenes.text: Ananya has one evening to revise Basic Electrical Engineering.
She works through a one-page sheet, then tests herself.

steps.title: DC
steps.body:
- V = IR; series/parallel; divider rules
- Δ→Y: product of adjacent/sum; Y→Δ: sum + product/third
- Thevenin V_oc, R_th; I_L = V_th/(R_th + R_L)
- P_max = V_th²/4R_th at R_L = R_th

steps.title: Single-phase AC
steps.body:
- V_rms = V_m/√2; FF 1.11; PF(crest) 1.414
- X_L = 2πfL; X_C = 1/2πfC; Z = R + j(X_L − X_C)
- P = VI cos φ; Q = VI sin φ; S = VI
- f₀ = 1/2π√LC; Q = ω₀L/R; BW = f₀/Q; Q_C = P(tan φ₁ − tan φ₂)

steps.title: How to use this sheet
steps.body:
- Cover the right-hand side of each formula and try to recall it.
- For every formula, say its conditions of validity aloud (units, assumptions, ranges).
- Re-solve one worked example from the matching unit without looking.

steps.title: Common slips to avoid
steps.body:
- Mixing units (kN vs N, mm vs m, km/h vs m/s, degrees vs radians).
- Using a formula outside its assumptions.
- Dropping signs or factors such as 2, ½, π or √3.

quiz.why: For a series R–L circuit Z = √(R² + X_L²) = √(64 + 36) = √100 = 10 Ω. Resistance and reactance add at right angles, not directly (14 Ω).

quiz.q: Y of 6 Ω each from Δ of
quiz.why: Delta to star conversion with equal resistors gives R_Y = R_Δ/3. So a star of 6 Ω each comes from a delta of 3 × 6 = 18 Ω.
Bandwidth = f₀/Q = 10 000/20 = 500 Hz. A higher Q means a narrower bandwidth.

- Cover the right-hand side of each formula and try to recall it.
- For every formula, say its conditions of validity aloud (units, assumptions, ranges).
- Re-solve one worked example from the matching unit without looking.

steps.title: Common slips to avoid
steps.body:
- Mixing units (kN vs N, mm vs m, km/h vs m/s, degrees vs radians).
- Using a formula outside its assumptions.
- Dropping signs or factors such as 2, ½, π or √3.

statements.s: Induction motor runs exactly at N_s.

quiz.why: N_s = 120f/P = 120 × 50/8 = 750 rpm. More poles means a slower synchronous speed.
In a delta connection each phase is connected directly across two lines, so line voltage equals phase voltage: 400 V.
Energy = power × time = 2 kW × 3 h = 6 kWh. Multiply, don't add.

scenes.text: Set a 30-minute timer and attempt every question before checking.
Read each explanation, even for the ones you got right.

steps.title: How to attempt
steps.body:
- Attempt easy questions first.
- For numericals write the formula, substitute with units, then simplify.
- Mark doubtful ones and return.

steps.title: Coverage
steps.body: This paper mixes every unit of Basic Electrical Engineering. Scores below 60% mean: re-read the unit whose questions you missed, then retake.

steps.title: Common mistakes in exams
steps.body:
- Skipping units and sign conventions.
- Copying a formula without checking its conditions of validity.
- Not reading 'NOT' / 'incorrect' in the question.

activity.prompt: Before the real exam
items: Formula sheet revised twice
One full mock done under time
Wrong answers re-solved without looking
Derivations listed in the syllabus practised once

quiz.q: Mock 1: Two 6 Ω in parallel then series 3 Ω
quiz.why: Two 6 Ω in parallel give 6×6/12 = 3 Ω. Adding the series 3 Ω gives 3 + 3 = 6 Ω.
RMS value = peak/√2 = 311/1.414 ≈ 220 V. The mains voltage of 220–230 V has this peak.
Z = √(4² + 3²) = 5 Ω, and pf = R/Z = 4/5 = 0.8. 0.6 would be the sine, not the power factor.
The turns ratio is 1000:100 = 10:1, so the voltage is divided by 10: 230/10 = 23 V.

quiz.q: Mock 1: Device protecting against shock via leakage
quiz.why: An RCCB detects earth leakage current (typically 30 mA) and trips fast to prevent shock. A fuse or MCB only responds to overload or short circuit, and an isolator just disconnects manually.

quiz.q: Mock 1: P_max for 10 V, 1 Ω source
quiz.why: Maximum power transfer happens when R_load = R_source = 1 Ω. Then I = 10/2 = 5 A, and P = I²R = 25 W, which is V²/(4R) = 100/4.

questions.q: Unit of inductance
questions.why: Inductance is measured in henry (H). Weber is flux, farad is capacitance and ohm is resistance.

questions.q: KCL relates
questions.why: Kirchhoff's current law says the currents meeting at a node add to zero, since charge cannot accumulate there. The loop-voltage law is KVL.

questions.q: Star line current equals
questions.why: In a star connection each line is connected in series with its phase winding, so line current equals phase current. The √3 factor applies to delta.

questions.q: Ideal transformer power
questions.why: An ideal transformer has no losses, so power in equals power out. Voltage and current may change but their product does not.

questions.q: X_L for 50 mH at 50 Hz
questions.why: X_L = 2πfL = 2π × 50 × 0.05 = 15.7 Ω. Remember to convert 50 mH to 0.05 H.

questions.q: Thevenin: 12 V with 2 Ω series and 2 Ω shunt ⇒ V_th, R_th
questions.why: With no load, V_th = 12 × 2/(2 + 2) = 6 V by the divider. R_th is the 2 Ω series in parallel with the 2 Ω shunt (source shorted) = 1 Ω.

questions.q: S for P = 8 kW, Q = 6 kVAR
questions.why: Apparent power S = √(P² + Q²) = √(64 + 36) = 10 kVA. P and Q are at right angles, so they do not add directly to 14.

questions.q: Rotor frequency at 1440 rpm, 4-pole, 50 Hz
f₀ of L = 10 mH, C = 10 µF
Assertion (A): Power factor correction reduces line current.  Reason (R): For the same active power, higher pf means lower apparent power.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: A is true: raising pf cuts the line current for the same load. R is also true and explains it: with the same P, I = P/(V cos φ), so a higher cos φ means lower current and lower apparent power.

questions.q: W₁ = 8 kW, W₂ = 4 kW ⇒ φ
Transformer 10 kVA, P_i 100 W, P_cu,FL 250 W, pf 0.8, half load η
Capacitor kVAR to improve 30 kW from 0.6 to 0.9 lag
questions.why: Q needed = P(tan φ₁ − tan φ₂) = 30(1.333 − 0.484) = 30 × 0.849 ≈ 25.5 kVAR, where tan φ₁ comes from pf 0.6 and tan φ₂ from pf 0.9.

questions.q: Case: A 3-phase 400 V delta heater has 3 elements of 40 Ω. Total power
questions.why: In delta each element has the 400 V line voltage, so P = 3V²/R = 3 × 400²/40 = 3 × 4000 = 12 000 W = 12 kW.

questions.q: Same elements reconnected in star
questions.why: In star each element gets only 400/√3 V, which is one-third the power of delta: 12 kW/3 = 4 kW.

questions.q: Mesh: 20 = 8I₁ − 4I₂; 0 = −4I₁ + 12I₂ ⇒ I₂
questions.why: From the second equation 4I₁ = 12I₂, so I₁ = 3I₂. Put that into the first: 20 = 8(3I₂) − 4I₂ = 20I₂, so I₂ = 1 A.

questions.q: DC shunt motor: 250 V, R_a 0.4 Ω, I_a 25 A at 1000 rpm. Speed at I_a = 50 A (same Φ)
questions.why: Speed ∝ back emf for the same flux. E_b = 250 − 25 × 0.4 = 240 V at first and 250 − 50 × 0.4 = 230 V at 50 A, so N = 1000 × 230/240 ≈ 958 rpm.

questions.q: Air-gap reluctance doubling (gap doubled) with same mmf makes gap flux
questions.why: Flux Φ = mmf/reluctance. If the air gap dominates the reluctance, doubling the gap doubles the reluctance, so the same mmf gives roughly half the flux.

questions.q: Energy stored in 10 µF at 100 V
questions.why: Energy = ½CV² = ½ × 10×10⁻⁶ × 100² = ½ × 10⁻⁵ × 10⁴ = 0.05 J. Check the µ factor carefully.
