courses.title: Engineering Mechanics · Unit 1 · Force systems and equilibrium
courses.summary: Resultant of coplanar concurrent and non-concurrent forces, moments, Varignon's theorem, couples, free-body diagrams, conditions of equilibrium, Lami's theorem and support reactions of beams.
outcomes: Resolve and combine forces into a resultant
Use moments, Varignon's theorem and couples
Draw correct free-body diagrams
Solve equilibrium problems with Lami's theorem and beam reactions
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

scenes.text: Two ropes pull a stuck car at different angles.
The car moves as if one single force — the resultant — acted on it.

steps.title: Resolution and composition
steps.body:
A force F at angle θ to the x-axis has components Fₓ = F cos θ, F_y = F sin θ. Resultant: R = √(ΣFₓ² + ΣF_y²), direction α = tan⁻¹(ΣF_y/ΣFₓ) (check the quadrant).
Parallelogram law (two forces P, Q at angle θ): R = √(P² + Q² + 2PQ cos θ), tan α = Q sin θ/(P + Q cos θ).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** P = 30 N, Q = 40 N at 90°: R = 50 N, α = tan⁻¹(40/30) = 53.1° from P.

**Example 2.** Forces 20 N at 0°, 30 N at 60°, 25 N at 150°: ΣFₓ = 20 + 15 − 21.65 = 13.35; ΣF_y = 0 + 25.98 + 12.5 = 38.48 ⇒ R = 40.7 N at 70.9°.

**Example 3.** Two equal forces P at 120°: R = √(P² + P² − P²) = P, bisecting the angle.

steps.title: Units and signs
steps.body: Take right and up as positive; write each component with its sign before adding. Draw a rough sketch to check the quadrant of R.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using sin for the x-component when the angle is measured from the x-axis.
- Taking tan⁻¹ without checking the quadrant.
- Adding force magnitudes arithmetically.

activity.prompt: Forces 6 kN and 8 kN act at right angles. Resultant (kN)?

quiz.q: Resultant of 3 N and 4 N at 90°
quiz.why: Forces at 90° form a right triangle, so the resultant is √(3² + 4²) = √25 = 5 N. Adding 3 + 4 = 7 N only works for forces in the same direction.

quiz.q: x-component of 100 N at 30° from x-axis
quiz.why: The component along x is F cos θ = 100 × cos 30° = 100 × 0.866 = 86.6 N. 50 N would be the sin 30° component.

quiz.q: Two equal forces at 180° give resultant
quiz.why: Two equal forces pointing in opposite directions along the same line cancel completely, so the resultant is 0.
The parallelogram law gives R = √(P² + Q² + 2PQ cos θ), where θ is the angle between the forces. It reduces to √(P² + Q²) only when θ = 90°.

quiz.q: Maximum resultant of two forces occurs at θ =
quiz.why: R is largest when cos θ = 1, that is θ = 0°, because then the forces act in the same direction and simply add: R = P + Q.

scenes.text: Pushing a door near its hinges barely moves it; at the handle it swings easily.
The turning effect — moment — is force × perpendicular distance.

steps.title: Moments
steps.body:
M = F × d (perpendicular distance from point to line of action); sign convention: anticlockwise positive (or state yours).
**Varignon's theorem:** moment of the resultant about a point = sum of moments of the components.
**Couple:** two equal, opposite, parallel forces separated by d; moment = Fd, same about every point; it produces pure rotation.
A force can be replaced by an equal force at another point plus a couple (force–couple system).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** 50 N at the end of a 0.4 m spanner, perpendicular: M = 20 N·m.

**Example 2.** 100 N at 30° to a 2 m bar at its end: M about the pivot = 100 sin 30° × 2 = 100 N·m (only the perpendicular component turns).

**Example 3.** Parallel forces 10 kN ↓ at x = 0, 20 kN ↓ at x = 3 m: R = 30 kN ↓; Varignon: 30 x̄ = 20 × 3 ⇒ x̄ = 2 m.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the slant distance instead of the perpendicular distance.
- Mixing sign conventions within one equation.
- Thinking a couple can be balanced by a single force (only by another couple).

activity.prompt: A 25 N force acts 0.8 m from a pivot (perpendicular). Moment (N·m)?

quiz.why: Moment = force × perpendicular distance from the point to the line of action. Distance measured along the force gives no turning effect.

quiz.q: Moment of a couple about any point
quiz.why: A couple has two equal and opposite parallel forces, and its moment Fd is the same about every point. It is a free vector.
Varignon's theorem says the moment of a resultant about any point equals the sum of the moments of its components about that point. It is the principle of moments.
A couple has equal and opposite forces, so the net force is zero and there is no translation. It only produces rotation.
Moment = force × length, so its unit is the newton-metre (N·m). N/m is something else, and J/s is power.

lessons.title: Free-body diagrams and equilibrium; Lami's theorem

scenes.text: A shop sign hangs from two chains at different angles.
Which chain carries more load? Draw the free-body diagram and apply equilibrium.

steps.title: Equilibrium
steps.body:
Coplanar: ΣFₓ = 0, ΣF_y = 0, ΣM = 0. **FBD:** isolate the body, show all external forces — weights, applied loads, reactions (normal, tension along strings, pin with two components, roller normal to surface).
**Lami's theorem:** for three concurrent forces in equilibrium, P/sin α = Q/sin β = R/sin γ, where each angle is between the other two forces.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** 200 N lamp hung by two strings making 30° and 60° with the ceiling. Angles between forces: between T₁ and T₂ = 90°, between T₂ and W = 150°, between T₁ and W = 120°.
T₁/sin 150° = T₂/sin 120° = 200/sin 90° ⇒ T₁ = 100 N (string at 30°), T₂ = 173.2 N (string at 60°).

**Example 2.** A 500 N sphere resting between two smooth inclined planes (60° and 30° to horizontal): the two normal reactions are 90° apart; Lami gives R₁ (on the 60° plane) = 500 sin 150°/sin 90° = 250 N and R₂ (on the 30° plane) = 500 sin 120°/sin 90° = 433 N.

steps.title: Check
steps.body: The steeper string (closer to vertical) always carries more of the weight — use this to sanity-check answers.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Leaving out reactions or the weight in the FBD.
- Using the angle with the horizontal directly in Lami's theorem (use the angle between the forces).
- Drawing tension pushing into the body.

activity.prompt: Steps to solve an equilibrium problem
items: Isolate the body
Draw the free-body diagram with all forces
Choose axes and sign convention
Write ΣFₓ = 0, ΣF_y = 0 (and ΣM = 0)
Solve and check the answer is physically sensible

quiz.why: Lami's theorem relates three concurrent, coplanar forces in equilibrium to the sines of the angles opposite them. It does not work for parallel forces or for more than three forces.

quiz.q: Equilibrium of a rigid body in 2-D needs
quiz.why: For a rigid body in a plane, equilibrium needs ΣFx = 0, ΣFy = 0 and ΣM = 0. Forces alone could still leave a net turning effect.
A string is flexible and cannot resist pushing or bending, so it can only pull. Hence it carries tension only.

quiz.q: Reaction from a smooth surface is
quiz.why: A smooth surface offers no friction, so the only contact force is the one perpendicular to the surface, the normal reaction.

quiz.q: In Example 1, the string at 60° to the ceiling carries
quiz.why: The steeper string (60° to the ceiling) carries more tension. In the stated set-up its value is 173.2 N, which is 100 N/sin 30° × sin 60°-type resolution larger than the 100 N, so 173.2 N is the matching choice.

scenes.text: A footbridge is pinned at one end and rests on rollers at the other.
Equilibrium equations give the support reactions for any crowd load.

steps.title: Supports and loads
steps.body:
Roller: one reaction normal to surface. Pin (hinge): two components. Fixed: two forces + a moment.
Loads: point load; UDL w (kN/m) → equivalent W = wL at its centre; uniformly varying load (triangle) → ½wL at L/3 from the larger end.
Statically determinate beams: simply supported, cantilever, overhanging.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Simply supported 6 m beam, 30 kN at 2 m from A: ΣM_A = 0 ⇒ R_B × 6 = 30 × 2 ⇒ R_B = 10 kN, R_A = 20 kN.

**Example 2.** 8 m beam with UDL 5 kN/m over the full span: R_A = R_B = 20 kN.

**Example 3.** Overhanging beam AB = 6 m, overhang BC = 2 m, 12 kN at C: ΣM_A: R_B × 6 = 12 × 8 ⇒ R_B = 16 kN ↑, R_A = −4 kN (acts downward).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Placing the UDL resultant anywhere but its centroid.
- Forgetting that a negative reaction means the assumed direction was wrong.
- Missing the fixing moment at a cantilever support.

activity.prompt: Simply supported beam 10 m, 50 kN at 4 m from A. R_B (kN)?

quiz.why: A roller support can only push or pull normal to the surface it rolls on, so it provides a single reaction.
A fixed support prevents both translation and rotation, so it gives two force components (horizontal and vertical) and a moment.
A uniformly distributed load becomes a single force w × L = 4 × 5 = 20 kN, acting at the centre of its length, 2.5 m from the end.
A triangular load has resultant equal to its area, ½wL, acting at the centroid, which is L/3 from the larger end.
options: ½wL at L/3 from the larger end

quiz.why: If the computed reaction is negative, the real direction is opposite to the direction you assumed. The calculation is not wrong.

questions.q: SI unit of force
questions.why: The SI unit of force is the newton (N). Pascal is pressure, joule is energy and watt is power.

questions.q: Resultant of two equal forces P at 90°
questions.why: For forces at 90°, R = √(P² + P²) = √2 P. Adding them (2P) would only be right for forces in the same direction.

questions.q: Moment of 10 N at 2 m perpendicular
questions.why: Moment = force × perpendicular distance = 10 × 2 = 20 N·m. Be careful to multiply, not add.

questions.q: Resultant of 5 N and 12 N at 90°
questions.why: R = √(5² + 12²) = √169 = 13 N. This is a 5-12-13 right triangle; 17 N would be adding the forces.

questions.q: Couple moment of 40 N forces 0.25 m apart
questions.why: The moment of a couple = force × perpendicular distance between the lines = 40 × 0.25 = 10 N·m.

questions.q: Simply supported 4 m beam with 10 kN at midspan: reactions
questions.why: A central load on a symmetric simply supported beam is shared equally by the supports, so each reaction is 10/2 = 5 kN.

questions.q: Assertion (A): A couple cannot be balanced by a single force.  Reason (R): A single force always produces a net translation tendency.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: A is true: a couple has only a turning effect, so one force can't balance it. R is false: a single force does tend to cause translation, but that isn't the reason. The real reason is that balancing needs an equal and opposite couple, and a single force produces a net force a couple does not have.

questions.q: Resultant of 10 N at 0° and 10 N at 60°
questions.why: For equal forces P at angle 60°, R = 2P cos(θ/2) = 2 × 10 × cos 30° = 17.32 N, acting along the bisector at 30°.

questions.q: Lamp 100 N on two strings each at 45° to horizontal: tension
questions.why: Vertical equilibrium: 2T sin 45° = 100, so T = 100/(2 × 0.707) = 70.7 N. Each string carries less than 100 N in vertical part but more than 50 N since it is inclined.

questions.q: Cantilever 3 m with 6 kN at free end: fixing moment
questions.why: At a fixed end the cantilever's moment is load × length = 6 kN × 3 m = 18 kN·m.

questions.q: Beam 6 m, UDL 2 kN/m over left 3 m only: R_B
questions.why: The 2 kN/m over 3 m is 6 kN acting at 1.5 m from A. Moments about A: R_B × 6 = 6 × 1.5, so R_B = 1.5 kN.

questions.q: Case: A 1200 N crate hangs from ropes at 30° and 45° to the horizontal. Tension in the 45° rope
questions.why: Lami: T₄₅ = 1200 sin 120°/sin 105° ≈ 1076 N (the 30° rope carries 1200 sin 135°/sin 105° ≈ 879 N).

questions.q: Overhanging beam AB = 4 m, overhang 1 m, 10 kN at the free end: R_A
questions.why: Moments about A: R_B × 4 = 10 × 5, so R_B = 12.5 kN up. Vertical balance: R_A = 10 − 12.5 = −2.5 kN, so R_A acts downward with 2.5 kN.

questions.q: Varignon: forces 4 kN at x = 1 m and 6 kN at x = 6 m (parallel, same sense). x̄ of resultant
questions.why: The resultant is 10 kN. Its position x̄ = (4 × 1 + 6 × 6)/10 = (4 + 36)/10 = 4 m, by taking moments (Varignon).

questions.q: Triangular load peak 6 kN/m at B on a 6 m simply supported beam (zero at A): R_B
questions.why: The load is ½ × 6 × 6 = 18 kN, acting at 2/3 of the span = 4 m from A. Moments about A: R_B × 6 = 18 × 4, so R_B = 12 kN.

courses.title: Engineering Mechanics · Unit 2 · Trusses and friction
courses.summary: Plane trusses: assumptions, method of joints and method of sections; laws of dry friction, angle of friction and repose, blocks on inclined planes, ladder friction, wedges and belt friction.
outcomes: Find member forces by method of joints and sections
Identify zero-force members
Apply Coulomb friction to blocks, ladders and wedges
Use the belt friction equation T₁/T₂ = e^(μθ)
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

scenes.text: Steel truss bridges use triangles because a triangle cannot change shape without changing side lengths.
Each member is either in tension or compression.

steps.title: Assumptions
steps.body: Members are straight, two-force members, pin-jointed; loads only at joints; weights neglected. Perfect (determinate) truss: m = 2j − 3 (m members, j joints).

steps.title: Method of joints
steps.body:
Find support reactions first. At a joint with at most two unknowns, apply ΣFₓ = 0, ΣF_y = 0. Assume tension (force pulling away from the joint); a negative answer means compression.
**Zero-force members:** (i) two non-collinear members at an unloaded joint — both zero; (ii) three members at an unloaded joint, two collinear — the third is zero.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Equilateral triangle truss, span 4 m, 10 kN at apex C, supports A (pin) and B (roller). R_A = R_B = 5 kN.
Joint A: F_AC sin 60° + 5 = 0 ⇒ F_AC = −5.77 kN (compression); F_AB + F_AC cos 60° = 0 ⇒ F_AB = 2.89 kN (tension). By symmetry F_BC = −5.77 kN.

**Example 2.** Check m = 2j − 3: triangle j = 3, m = 3 ✔.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Starting at a joint with three unknowns.
- Forgetting reactions.
- Mislabelling compression as tension (keep the 'away from joint' convention).

activity.prompt: Member nature in Example 1

quiz.why: A perfect (just-stiff) truss satisfies m = 2j − 3, where m is the number of members and j the number of joints. More members make it redundant, fewer make it a mechanism.
Truss members are two-force members joined by pins, with loads applied at joints. They carry only axial tension or compression, not bending or shear.

quiz.q: Unloaded joint with two non-collinear members: forces
quiz.why: At an unloaded joint of two non-collinear members, the forces cannot balance unless both are zero. Equilibrium needs both force components to vanish.
A negative result means the actual force acts opposite to the assumed tension, i.e. it pushes on the joints, so the member is in compression.

quiz.q: Members for j = 6 in a perfect truss
quiz.why: m = 2j − 3 = 2 × 6 − 3 = 9 members.

scenes.text: An inspector only needs the force in one middle member of a long bridge truss.
Cut through it and use moment equilibrium — no need to solve every joint.

steps.title: Method
steps.body: Cut the truss through at most three members whose forces are unknown (not all concurrent). Take one part as a free body. Use ΣM about the intersection point of two unknown members to find the third directly.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Pratt truss with panels 3 m, height 4 m, R_A = 30 kN, loads 20 kN at the first bottom joint. Cut through top chord member, diagonal and bottom chord in panel 2. Moment about the top joint above the first bottom joint: F_bottom × 4 = 30 × 3 ⇒ F_bottom = 22.5 kN (tension).

**Example 2.** In the same cut, vertical equilibrium: 30 − 20 − F_diag sin θ = 0 with sin θ = 4/5 ⇒ F_diag = 12.5 kN.

steps.title: Choose the moment centre
steps.body: Pick the point where two of the cut members meet — their forces vanish from the moment equation.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Cutting more than three unknown members.
- Including loads from the other side of the cut.
- Using the slant distance for moments.

activity.prompt: In a cut, moment equation F × 3 = 45 × 2 (kN, m). Find F (kN).

quiz.q: Method of sections cuts through at most
quiz.why: A section cut should pass through at most three members with unknown forces, because only three equilibrium equations (ΣFx, ΣFy, ΣM) are available in the plane.
Take moments about the point where two cut members meet. Their forces have no moment about it, so the third unknown can be found directly.

quiz.q: Method of sections is efficient for
quiz.why: The method of sections is efficient when you need the force in only a few particular members, since you don't have to solve every joint.

quiz.q: Diagonal force from vertical equilibrium uses
quiz.why: Vertical equilibrium of a cut panel involves the vertical component of the diagonal, which balances the shear of the panel. Its length and moment are not used in that equation.
Both methods usually need the support reactions found first, from equilibrium of the whole truss. After that the members can be solved.

lessons.title: Laws of friction and inclined planes

scenes.text: Workers slide boxes down a ramp; at a certain slope they start sliding on their own.
That slope is the angle of repose — equal to the angle of friction.

steps.title: Coulomb friction
steps.body:
Limiting friction F = μN (static μ_s), kinetic F_k = μ_k N (μ_k < μ_s). Friction opposes impending/actual motion, independent of contact area (dry surfaces).
Angle of friction φ: tan φ = μ. Angle of repose α = φ (block on its own just starts to slide).

steps.title: Block on an inclined plane (angle α)
steps.body:
Without applied force, block stays if tan α ≤ μ.
Force parallel to plane to move up: P = W(sin α + μ cos α); to prevent slipping down: P = W(sin α − μ cos α).
Horizontal force to push up: P = W tan(α + φ).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** 500 N block on a horizontal floor, μ = 0.3: force to start sliding = 150 N.

**Example 2.** 1000 N on a 30° incline, μ = 0.25, force parallel to plane: up: 1000(0.5 + 0.2165) = 716.5 N; to hold: 1000(0.5 − 0.2165) = 283.5 N.

**Example 3.** Pull at angle θ on a level floor: P = μW/(cos θ + μ sin θ); minimum when θ = φ.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Taking N = W on an incline (it is W cos α) or when the pull has a vertical component.
- Pointing friction in the direction of motion.
- Using μ_k for impending motion.

activity.label: Incline angle for a block with μ = 0.4 (φ ≈ 21.8°)

bands.text: Below φ: friction holds the block — it stays at rest.
Near 21.8° the block is on the verge of sliding (angle of repose).
Above φ: the block slides down by itself.

quiz.why: Coulomb's law of dry friction gives limiting friction F = μN, where N is the normal reaction. It is not always μW; that only holds on a level floor with no other vertical force.
The angle of repose, where a block just starts to slide, has tan α = μ, the same as tan φ for the angle of friction. So the two angles are equal.
Dry friction depends on the normal force and on the materials and roughness. It does not depend on the apparent area of contact.

quiz.q: Normal reaction on an incline (no other force)
quiz.why: On an incline with no other force, the normal reaction balances the component of weight perpendicular to the plane: N = W cos α. W sin α acts along the plane.
Experiments show kinetic friction is usually somewhat less than static friction, so it's easier to keep something sliding than to start it.

scenes.text: A rope wrapped a few turns round a post holds a ship with a small pull.
Belt friction grows exponentially with wrap angle.

steps.title: Ladder friction
steps.body:
Ladder of weight W, length L, against a wall at angle θ to the floor. Unknowns: floor N_A, F_A; wall N_B, F_B. Use ΣFₓ = 0, ΣF_y = 0, ΣM_A = 0 with F = μN at both contacts for limiting state (or μ_wall = 0 for a smooth wall).
Smooth wall, rough floor μ: tan θ_min = 1/(2μ) for a uniform ladder alone.

steps.title: Wedges and belts
steps.body:
Wedges: draw FBDs of wedge and block; friction on every sliding face; solve simultaneously (often with Lami or force polygons).
**Belt friction (flat belt, impending slip):** T₁/T₂ = e^(μθ), θ in radians, T₁ tight side. Power P = (T₁ − T₂)v. V-belt: T₁/T₂ = e^(μθ/sin(β/2)) (β = groove angle).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Uniform ladder, smooth wall, floor μ = 0.5: tan θ_min = 1 ⇒ θ_min = 45°.

**Example 2.** Rope 2 turns round a post (θ = 4π), μ = 0.3: T₁/T₂ = e^(3.77) ≈ 43.4 — a 10 N pull holds 434 N.

**Example 3.** Belt μ = 0.3, wrap 180°, T₁ = 2000 N: T₂ = 2000/e^(0.942) = 780 N; at v = 10 m/s, P = 12.2 kW.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- θ in degrees in e^(μθ).
- Wrong direction of friction at the wall for a slipping ladder (it opposes the top sliding down — acts upward).
- Swapping tight and slack sides.

activity.prompt: Belt: μ = 0.25, wrap = π rad, T₂ = 1000 N. T₁ = 1000·e^(μθ) (N)?

quiz.why: The belt (capstan) friction equation is T₁/T₂ = e^(μθ). The tension ratio grows exponentially with the wrap angle and friction.

quiz.q: θ in the belt equation is in
quiz.why: In e^(μθ) the angle must be in radians, because the exponent is a pure number. Using degrees would give a wrong ratio.
The belt does net work from the difference in the tensions, so P = (T₁ − T₂)v. Adding the tensions would count the slack side wrongly.

quiz.q: Smooth wall, μ = 0.25 at floor: tan θ_min
quiz.why: For a ladder against a smooth wall, friction at the floor must give H = μR. Moments yield tan θ = 1/(2μ) = 1/(2 × 0.25) = 2.
The wedge shape of a V-belt makes the normal force on the sides larger than the pulling force, so the grip is higher: effective μ is μ/sin(β/2).

questions.q: Zero-force members exist to
questions.why: Zero-force members help stabilise the truss and keep long members from buckling, and they can carry load when the loading changes. They are not useless.
options: stabilise the truss / carry other load cases

questions.q: Coefficient of friction μ =
questions.why: The coefficient of friction is the ratio of limiting friction to normal reaction: μ = F/N.

questions.q: Perfect truss with 5 joints has members
questions.why: A perfect truss has m = 2j − 3 = 2 × 5 − 3 = 7 members.

questions.q: Block 200 N, μ = 0.4 on level floor: force to start
questions.why: On a level floor N = W = 200 N, so the force to start motion is μW = 0.4 × 200 = 80 N.

questions.q: Angle of repose for μ = 1
questions.why: Angle of repose = tan⁻¹ μ = tan⁻¹ 1 = 45°.

questions.q: Force to drag 600 N up 30° incline (μ = 0.2), parallel
Assertion (A): A member of a truss carries only axial force.  Reason (R): Loads act only at pin joints and members are pin-connected.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: A is true: members carry only axial force. R is true and is the reason: if the members are pin-connected and loads act only at the joints, each member is a two-force member, so no bending occurs.

questions.q: Triangle truss: apex load 20 kN, equilateral, member AC force
questions.why: Each support reaction is 10 kN (half of 20). At the support joint, the member AC at 60° gives F sin 60° = 10, so F = 10/0.866 = 11.55 kN. It pushes into the joint, so it is in compression.

questions.q: Belt wrap 210°, μ = 0.3: T₁/T₂
Uniform ladder, smooth wall, floor μ = 0.3: minimum angle with floor
questions.why: For a smooth wall, tan θ = 1/(2μ) = 1/0.6 = 1.667, so θ = tan⁻¹ 1.667 ≈ 59°. Using 0.3 directly would give 73°, which is wrong.

questions.q: Case: A 2 kN crate must be held on a 40° ramp with μ = 0.35. Minimum parallel holding force
questions.why: Down-slope component = 2 sin 40° ≈ 1.286 kN; maximum friction = 0.35 × 2 cos 40° ≈ 0.536 kN. Since friction alone cannot hold the crate, the minimum up-slope force = 1.286 − 0.536 ≈ 0.75 kN.

questions.q: Method of sections: moment about joint gives F × 4 = 60 × 6 − 20 × 3. F
Power by belt: T₁ = 1500 N, T₂ = 600 N, v = 20 m/s
Rope with 3 full turns, μ = 0.2: amplification e^(μθ)
questions.why: Three full turns give θ = 3 × 2π = 6π rad. e^(μθ) = e^(0.2 × 18.85) = e^3.77 ≈ 43, so a small holding force balances a much larger load.

questions.q: Pull at angle θ on level floor: least force needed when
questions.why: Pulling at angle θ, P = μW/(cos θ + μ sin θ). It is smallest when cos θ + μ sin θ is largest, which occurs at tan θ = μ, i.e. θ equals the angle of friction.

courses.title: Engineering Mechanics · Unit 3 · Centroid and moment of inertia
courses.summary: Centre of gravity and centroid of lines and areas, standard shapes and composite sections, area moment of inertia, parallel- and perpendicular-axis theorems, radius of gyration, and mass moment of inertia of common bodies.
outcomes: Find centroids of standard and composite areas
Compute area moments of inertia of standard sections
Apply parallel and perpendicular axis theorems
Use radius of gyration and mass moments of inertia
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

scenes.text: A triangular signboard balances on one point — its centroid.
For a uniform plate, centre of gravity and centroid coincide.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body: x̄ = ∫x dA/A, ȳ = ∫y dA/A. Axis of symmetry always contains the centroid.

steps.title: Standard results
steps.body:
- Rectangle b × h: (b/2, h/2)
- Triangle: h/3 from base (2h/3 from apex)
- Semicircle radius r: 4r/(3π) from diameter
- Quarter circle: (4r/3π, 4r/3π)
- Circular arc (semicircular wire): 2r/π from diameter
- Right cone (solid): h/4 from base; hemisphere (solid): 3r/8 from base

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1 (derivation, triangle).** Strip at height y: width b(h − y)/h; ȳ = ∫₀ʰ y·b(h − y)/h dy/(bh/2) = (bh²/6)/(bh/2) = h/3.

**Example 2.** Semicircle r = 6 cm: ȳ = 4·6/(3π) = 2.55 cm from the diameter.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Measuring the triangle centroid from the apex as h/3.
- Using 4r/3π for a semicircular wire (it is 2r/π).
- Forgetting symmetry gives one coordinate immediately.

activity.prompt: Match shape with centroid distance

quiz.why: A rectangle is symmetric about both its centre lines, so its centroid is at the intersection, i.e. its centre.

quiz.q: Triangle height 9 cm: centroid from base
quiz.why: The centroid of a triangle lies at one-third of its height from the base: 9/3 = 3 cm.

quiz.q: Semicircle r = 3π cm: ȳ from diameter
quiz.why: A semicircle's centroid is 4r/(3π) from the diameter. With r = 3π, ȳ = 4 × 3π/(3π) = 4 cm.
The centroid always lies on any axis of symmetry of the shape, because each side balances the other.

quiz.q: Centroid of a solid cone from base
quiz.why: A solid cone's centroid is at h/4 from its base (3h/4 from the apex). h/3 is the triangle's value.

scenes.text: T-beams and L-angles in buildings are composite shapes.
Split into rectangles, take moments of areas, divide by total area.

steps.title: Method
steps.body: x̄ = ΣAᵢxᵢ/ΣAᵢ, ȳ = ΣAᵢyᵢ/ΣAᵢ. Holes and cut-outs are negative areas. Use a table: part, A, x, y, Ax, Ay.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1 (T-section).** Flange 100 × 20 mm on top of web 20 × 80 mm (total height 100 mm). From the bottom: web A = 1600, y = 40; flange A = 2000, y = 90. ȳ = (64 000 + 180 000)/3600 = 67.8 mm.

**Example 2 (L-section).** 100 × 10 vertical leg + 90 × 10 horizontal leg (total 100 × 100): vertical A = 1000, (5, 50); horizontal A = 900, (55, 5). x̄ = (5000 + 49 500)/1900 = 28.7 mm; ȳ = (50 000 + 4500)/1900 = 28.7 mm.

**Example 3 (plate with hole).** 200 × 100 rectangle with a 40 mm diameter hole centred at (150, 50): x̄ = (20 000 × 100 − 1256.6 × 150)/(20 000 − 1256.6) = 96.6 mm.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Overlapping areas counted twice in an L-section.
- Adding a hole's area instead of subtracting.
- Measuring yᵢ from different reference lines.

activity.prompt: T-section (flange 100×20 on web 20×80): ȳ from bottom in mm (1 decimal)

quiz.why: The centroid of a composite shape is x̄ = ΣAx/ΣA, the area-weighted average of the parts' centroids.
A hole removes area, so in composite calculations it is treated as a negative area.
A symmetric I-section is symmetric about its mid-depth horizontal axis, so its centroid is at mid-depth.

quiz.q: Equal-leg L-section has x̄ = ȳ because
quiz.why: An equal-leg L-section is symmetric about the line at 45° to its legs, so the centroid is equally far from both outer edges, x̄ = ȳ.
options: it is symmetric about the 45° line

quiz.q: Removing material from one side moves the centroid
quiz.why: Removing material from one side leaves less area there, so the centroid shifts away from that side, toward the remaining material.

lessons.title: Area moment of inertia and theorems

scenes.text: Floor beams are I-shaped, not solid rectangles.
Putting material far from the neutral axis gives a large moment of inertia — stiffness for less steel.

steps.title: Standard second moments of area
steps.body:
- Rectangle about centroidal axis parallel to b: I = bh³/12; about base: bh³/3
- Triangle about centroidal axis parallel to base: bh³/36; about base: bh³/12
- Circle about diameter: πd⁴/64 = πr⁴/4; polar J = πd⁴/32
- Semicircle about diameter: πr⁴/8; about centroidal axis: 0.11r⁴

steps.title: Theorems
steps.body:
**Parallel axis:** I_AB = I_G + Ah² (h = distance between parallel axes; one must pass through the centroid).
**Perpendicular axis (plane areas):** I_z = Iₓ + I_y.
Radius of gyration k = √(I/A).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Rectangle 100 × 200 mm (h = 200): I_xx = 100 × 200³/12 = 6.67×10⁷ mm⁴; k = √(I/A) = 57.7 mm.

**Example 2.** Same about the base: I = 6.67×10⁷ + 20 000 × 100² = 2.67×10⁸ mm⁴ (= bh³/3 ✔).

**Example 3.** Circle d = 100 mm: I = π(100)⁴/64 = 4.91×10⁶ mm⁴; J = 9.82×10⁶ mm⁴.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the parallel axis theorem between two non-centroidal axes directly.
- bh³ vs hb³ — the cube goes on the dimension perpendicular to the axis.
- Applying the perpendicular axis theorem to 3-D bodies (it is for plane laminas).

activity.prompt: Moments of inertia
activity.text: Rectangle about its centroidal axis: I = bh^___/12; circle about a diameter: I = πd⁴/___.

quiz.why: The parallel axis theorem: I = I_G + Ah², where h is the distance between the axes. It adds a positive term when moving from the centroid.
For a triangle, the second moment about its base is bh³/12, and about the centroidal axis it is bh³/36.
The polar moment of a circle is J = πd⁴/32, which is twice I = πd⁴/64 about a diameter.
The radius of gyration is k = √(I/A), the distance at which the whole area would give the same I.
For a plane area, the perpendicular axis theorem says I_z = I_x + I_y, where z is perpendicular to the plane.

lessons.title: MOI of composite sections and mass moment of inertia

scenes.text: A flywheel stores energy because its mass is far from the axis.
Mass moment of inertia I = Σmr² controls how hard it is to spin up.

steps.title: Composite sections
steps.body: Find the centroid; for each part, I_part about the centroidal axis of the whole = I_own + A d²; sum (subtract holes).

steps.title: Mass moments of inertia
steps.body:
- Slender rod about centre: mL²/12; about end: mL²/3
- Disc/cylinder about axis: mr²/2; ring: mr²
- Solid sphere: 2mr²/5; hollow sphere: 2mr²/3
- Rectangular plate about centroidal axis ⊥ plane: m(a² + b²)/12
Rotational KE = ½Iω².

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using distances from the bottom instead of from the composite centroid in Ad².
- Mixing area MOI (m⁴) and mass MOI (kg m²).
- Forgetting to convert rpm to rad/s.

activity.prompt: Mass MOI of a 2 kg rod of length 3 m about its end (kg·m²)?

quiz.q: MOI of ring about its axis
quiz.why: All the mass of a thin ring lies at distance r from its axis, so I = mr², not a fraction of it.
A solid sphere's moment of inertia about a diameter is (2/5)mr². mr² is for a ring.
A thin rod about its centre has I = mL²/12; about one end it is mL²/3.
Rotational kinetic energy is ½Iω², the rotational counterpart of ½mv².

quiz.q: In composite I, d is measured from
quiz.why: In I = I_G + Ad², the distance d is measured from the composite's own centroid to each part's centroid, so the result is about the composite's centroidal axis.

questions.q: Centroid of a triangle from apex
questions.why: A triangle's centroid is h/3 from the base, so from the apex it is 2h/3.

questions.q: Unit of area moment of inertia
questions.why: Second moment of area has dimensions length × length³ = length⁴, so its SI unit is m⁴.

questions.q: Disc MOI about axis
questions.why: A uniform disc about its axis has I = ½mr². A ring has mr² and a sphere (2/5)mr².

questions.q: I of 60 × 120 mm rectangle about centroidal axis ∥ 60 side
questions.why: For a rectangle, I = bh³/12 with the dimension perpendicular to the axis cubed: 60 × 120³/12 = 60 × 1 728 000/12 = 8.64×10⁶ mm⁴.

questions.q: Quarter circle r = 3 cm: centroid coordinates
questions.why: A quarter circle has centroid 4r/(3π) from each straight edge = 4 × 3/(3π) = 4/π ≈ 1.27 cm in both x and y.

questions.q: k for a circle of diameter d
Assertion (A): I about any axis is least about the parallel centroidal axis.  Reason (R): I = I_G + Ah² with Ah² ≥ 0.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: A is true: among parallel axes, I is least about the centroidal one. R is true and explains it: I = I_G + Ah² and the Ah² term is never negative, so any shift adds to I_G.

questions.q: Rectangle 200 × 100 with 40 mm hole at (150, 50): x̄
questions.why: Net area = 20 000 − π(20)² ≈ 18 743 mm². x̄ = (20 000 × 100 − 1257 × 150)/18 743 ≈ 96.6 mm. The hole is on the right, so the centroid moves left of 100.

questions.q: I of triangle b = 60, h = 90 about centroidal axis ∥ base
questions.why: A triangle about its centroidal axis parallel to the base has I = bh³/36 = 60 × 90³/36 = 60 × 729 000/36 = 1.215×10⁶ mm⁴.

questions.q: Hollow circle D = 100, d = 80 mm: I about diameter
questions.why: Subtract the inner circle's I from the outer one: π(D⁴ − d⁴)/64 = π(10⁸ − 4.096×10⁷)/64 ≈ 2.90×10⁶ mm⁴.

questions.q: Case: A 30 kg solid disc flywheel of radius 0.5 m spins at 300 rpm. KE
questions.why: For a disc I = ½mr² = ½ × 30 × 0.25 = 3.75 kg·m². ω = 300 × 2π/60 = 31.4 rad/s, so KE = ½Iω² = ½ × 3.75 × 986 ≈ 1.85 kJ.

questions.q: I-section: flanges 100 × 10 each, web 10 × 100 (overall depth 120). I about centroidal x-axis
questions.why: Each flange: 100 × 10³/12 + 1000 × 55² = 8333 + 3 025 000, so two flanges ≈ 6.07×10⁶. The web gives 10 × 100³/12 = 0.83×10⁶. Total ≈ 6.90×10⁶ mm⁴.

questions.q: Polar MOI of a 50 mm diameter shaft
questions.why: Polar moment of a solid shaft J = πd⁴/32 = π × 50⁴/32 = π × 6.25×10⁶/32 ≈ 6.14×10⁵ mm⁴.

questions.q: Centroid of semicircle r = 10 cm sitting on its diameter on top of a 20 × 10 cm rectangle (diameter on top edge): ȳ from bottom
questions.why: Rectangle 200 cm² at 5 cm; semicircle 157.1 cm² at 10 + 4.24 = 14.24 cm ⇒ (1000 + 2237)/357.1 ≈ 9.07 cm.

questions.q: Mass MOI of rectangular plate 2 kg, 0.3 × 0.4 m about centroidal axis ⊥ plane
questions.why: For a rectangular plate about the axis perpendicular to its plane through the centre, I = m(a² + b²)/12 = 2(0.09 + 0.16)/12 = 0.0417 kg·m².

courses.title: Engineering Mechanics · Unit 4 · Kinematics and kinetics of particles
courses.summary: Rectilinear and curvilinear motion, projectiles, relative velocity, Newton's second law and D'Alembert's principle, work–energy principle, impulse–momentum and collisions with coefficient of restitution.
outcomes: Use equations of motion and motion graphs
Analyse projectiles and relative motion
Apply Newton's law, D'Alembert, work–energy
Solve impulse–momentum and impact problems
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

scenes.text: A metro train decelerates uniformly from 72 km/h to rest at a platform.
Equations of uniform acceleration give the braking distance.

steps.title: Equations
steps.body:
Uniform acceleration: v = u + at; s = ut + ½at²; v² = u² + 2as; s_nth = u + a(2n − 1)/2.
Variable acceleration: v = ds/dt, a = dv/dt = v dv/ds.
Graphs: slope of s–t = v; slope of v–t = a; area under v–t = displacement; area under a–t = change in velocity.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** 72 km/h = 20 m/s to rest in 40 s: a = −0.5 m/s²; s = 20 × 40 − ½ × 0.5 × 1600 = 400 m.

**Example 2.** Ball thrown up at 19.6 m/s: time to top 2 s; max height 19.6 m (g = 9.8).

**Example 3.** a = 6t m/s², v(0) = 2: v = 3t² + 2, s = t³ + 2t (s₀ = 0); at t = 2 s: v = 14 m/s, s = 12 m.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using constant-acceleration formulas when a varies.
- Mixing km/h and m/s (÷ 3.6).
- Sign of g when taking upward positive.

activity.prompt: Car from 0 to 30 m/s in 10 s (uniform). Distance covered (m)?

quiz.q: Area under a v–t graph gives
quiz.why: Velocity is the rate of change of displacement, so the area under a velocity–time graph (the integral of v dt) gives displacement.
To change km/h to m/s divide by 3.6: 72/3.6 = 20 m/s.

quiz.q: a = v dv/ds is useful when
quiz.why: Using a = v dv/ds, from the chain rule, helps when acceleration is given as a function of position s instead of time.
options: a is given as a function of s

quiz.q: Time to reach the top for u = 29.4 m/s (g = 9.8)
quiz.why: At the top v = 0, so 0 = u − gt and t = u/g = 29.4/9.8 = 3 s.
The slope of a displacement–time graph is ds/dt, which is velocity.

scenes.text: A firefighter aims a jet at a third-floor window.
The jet follows a parabola — projectile motion.

steps.title: Projectile (launched at u, angle θ, level ground, no air drag)
steps.body: Time of flight T = 2u sin θ/g; max height H = u² sin²θ/(2g); range R = u² sin 2θ/g (maximum at 45°: R_max = u²/g). Trajectory y = x tan θ − gx²/(2u²cos²θ). Complementary angles (θ and 90° − θ) give equal ranges.

steps.title: Relative velocity
steps.body: v_A/B = v_A − v_B (vector subtraction). Rain–man problems: umbrella tilt angle tan α = v_man/v_rain. River crossing: shortest time — head straight across; shortest path — head upstream so the resultant is perpendicular.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** u = 20 m/s at 30°: T = 2.04 s; H = 5.10 m; R = 35.3 m.

**Example 2.** Stone thrown horizontally at 10 m/s from a 19.6 m cliff: t = 2 s, horizontal distance 20 m.

**Example 3.** River 100 m wide flowing at 3 m/s; boat 5 m/s in still water. Shortest time: 20 s, drift 60 m. Zero drift: heading upstream with sin α = 3/5; crossing speed 4 m/s ⇒ 25 s.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using R = u² sin 2θ/g for unequal launch/landing heights.
- Forgetting horizontal velocity stays constant (no drag).
- Adding velocities instead of subtracting for relative velocity.

activity.label: Launch angle for a projectile at 20 m/s

bands.text: Low angle: short flight time, flatter path.
High angle: long flight, high peak, range shrinks (complements give equal range).

quiz.why: Range R = u² sin 2θ/g is largest when sin 2θ = 1, so 2θ = 90° and θ = 45° on level ground.

quiz.q: Horizontal velocity of a projectile (no drag)
quiz.why: With no air drag no horizontal force acts, so the horizontal velocity stays constant during the flight.
Ranges are equal for complementary angles, since sin 2θ = sin(180° − 2θ). The partner of 30° is 90° − 30° = 60°.
Time of flight is T = 2u sin θ/g, twice the time to reach the top (u sin θ/g).

quiz.q: Relative velocity of A w.r.t. B
quiz.why: Relative velocity of A with respect to B is the velocity of A minus the velocity of B: v_A − v_B (a vector difference).

lessons.title: Newton's second law, D'Alembert's principle and work–energy

scenes.text: A lift of 800 kg accelerates upward at 1 m/s².
Cable tension = m(g + a) — more than its weight.

steps.title: Kinetics
steps.body:
ΣF = ma. **D'Alembert:** add an inertia force −ma and treat the problem as static equilibrium: ΣF − ma = 0.
Connected bodies: write ΣF = ma for each with common acceleration and string tension.

steps.title: Work–energy
steps.body:
Work W = ∫F·ds; KE = ½mv²; PE = mgh; spring energy ½kx².
Work–energy principle: net work = ΔKE. Power P = Fv. With only conservative forces: KE + PE = constant.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Lift 800 kg, a = 1 m/s² up: T = 800(9.81 + 1) = 8648 N.

**Example 2.** Atwood: 5 kg and 3 kg over a smooth pulley: a = (5 − 3)g/8 = 2.45 m/s²; T = 3(9.81 + 2.45) = 36.8 N.

**Example 3.** 2 kg block slides 5 m down a smooth 30° incline from rest: v = √(2g × 5 sin 30°) = √49.05 = 7.0 m/s. With μ = 0.2: net work = mg(sin 30° − 0.2 cos 30°) × 5 = 2(9.81)(0.5 − 0.173)(5) = 32.1 J ⇒ v = 5.67 m/s.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing T = mg for an accelerating lift.
- Forgetting friction's negative work.
- Using mass instead of weight in force balances.

activity.prompt: Lift 500 kg accelerating downward at 2 m/s² (g = 9.81). Cable tension (N)?

quiz.why: D'Alembert's inertia force is −ma, acting opposite to the acceleration. Adding it turns a dynamics problem into a statics one.
The work–energy principle: net work done on a body equals its change in kinetic energy.
Power is the rate of doing work, P = F·v for a force along the direction of motion.
The energy stored in a spring stretched by x is ½kx², the area under the F = kx line.
Atwood machine: a = (m₂ − m₁)g/(m₁ + m₂) = (6 − 4)g/10 = 2g/10 = g/5.

scenes.text: Crumple zones and airbags increase the time of impact.
Same change in momentum over a longer time means a smaller force.

steps.title: Impulse–momentum
steps.body: Impulse J = ∫F dt = Δ(mv). Average force F = Δp/Δt. Conservation of linear momentum when no external impulse: m₁u₁ + m₂u₂ = m₁v₁ + m₂v₂.

steps.title: Direct central impact
steps.body:
Coefficient of restitution e = (v₂ − v₁)/(u₁ − u₂) (separation/approach). e = 1 perfectly elastic (KE conserved), e = 0 perfectly plastic (bodies move together), 0 < e < 1 typical.
Ball dropped from h bounces to e²h.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** 0.15 kg ball at 30 m/s caught in 0.05 s: F = 0.15 × 30/0.05 = 90 N.

**Example 2.** 2 kg at 6 m/s hits 4 kg at rest, e = 0.5: momentum 12 = 2v₁ + 4v₂; v₂ − v₁ = 3 ⇒ v₂ = 3 m/s, v₁ = 0. KE loss = 36 − 18 = 18 J.

**Example 3.** Ball dropped from 2 m rebounds to 1.28 m: e = √(1.28/2) = 0.8.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Sign errors with directions of velocity.
- Assuming KE is conserved in all collisions.
- Using e with speeds instead of velocities (signs matter).

activity.prompt: Ball dropped from 5 m, e = 0.6. Rebound height (m)?

quiz.why: Impulse = force × time = change in momentum (the impulse–momentum theorem). It is not energy or work.
A perfectly plastic impact means the bodies stick together, so there is no rebound and the coefficient of restitution e = 0.
A perfectly elastic collision has e = 1 and conserves both momentum and kinetic energy. Momentum is conserved in every isolated collision.
Airbags lengthen the time of impact. Since F = Δp/Δt, for the same change in momentum, a longer Δt means a smaller force.

quiz.q: Rebound height for e = 0.5 from 4 m
quiz.why: For a bounce, the rebound speed is e times the impact speed, so rebound height = e²h = 0.25 × 4 = 1 m.

questions.q: SI unit of momentum
questions.why: Momentum = mass × velocity, so the unit is kg·m/s. J is energy, N is force and W is power.

questions.q: Range is maximum at
questions.why: On level ground range ∝ sin 2θ, which is greatest at θ = 45°.

questions.q: KE of 2 kg at 3 m/s
questions.why: KE = ½mv² = ½ × 2 × 3² = 9 J. Don't forget to square the speed.

questions.q: Distance in 4th second for u = 0, a = 2 m/s²
questions.why: Distance in the nth second = u + a(2n − 1)/2 = 0 + 2 × 7/2 = 7 m. This differs from the total distance in 4 s, which is 16 m.

questions.q: Projectile u = 30 m/s at 60°: max height (g = 9.81)
Recoil of 4 kg gun firing 20 g bullet at 400 m/s
questions.why: Momentum is conserved: bullet momentum = 0.02 × 400 = 8 kg·m/s, so gun recoil speed = 8/4 = 2 m/s in the opposite direction.

questions.q: Assertion (A): In a perfectly inelastic collision, kinetic energy is not conserved.  Reason (R): Some kinetic energy becomes heat, sound and deformation.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: A is true: in a perfectly inelastic collision the bodies stick together and kinetic energy is lost. R is true and explains it: the lost KE becomes heat, sound and deformation. Momentum is still conserved.

questions.q: Block 10 kg pulled by 50 N on floor with μ = 0.2 (g = 9.81): acceleration
Car 1000 kg at 20 m/s brakes to rest in 50 m: average braking force
questions.why: The work–energy principle gives F × s = ΔKE = ½ × 1000 × 400 = 2×10⁵ J, so F = 2×10⁵/50 = 4000 N.

questions.q: Stone thrown horizontally at 15 m/s from 44.1 m height lands after
questions.why: Fall time t = √(2h/g) = √(88.2/9.81) = 3 s. The horizontal speed is constant, so range = 15 × 3 = 45 m.

questions.q: Case: A 1500 kg car at 15 m/s rear-ends a 1000 kg car at rest; they lock together. Common speed
questions.why: Momentum is conserved in a locking collision: 1500 × 15 = 22 500 = (1500 + 1000)v, so v = 22 500/2500 = 9 m/s.

questions.q: Energy lost in that collision
questions.why: Initial KE = ½ × 1500 × 15² = 168.75 kJ, final KE = ½ × 2500 × 9² = 101.25 kJ. Energy lost = 168.75 − 101.25 = 67.5 kJ.

questions.q: a = −kv (k = 0.5 s⁻¹), v₀ = 10 m/s. Total distance before stopping
questions.why: With a = v dv/ds = −kv, dv/ds = −k, so v falls linearly with s. It reaches zero at s = v₀/k = 10/0.5 = 20 m, a finite distance.

questions.q: Spring k = 2000 N/m compressed 0.1 m launches 0.5 kg ball (smooth). Speed
questions.why: Spring energy ½kx² = ½ × 2000 × 0.01 = 10 J becomes KE, so ½ × 0.5 × v² = 10, v² = 40, v ≈ 6.32 m/s.

questions.q: 2 kg at 5 m/s hits 3 kg at −2 m/s head-on, e = 1. Velocity of 2 kg after
questions.why: For e = 1 the formula gives v₁ = [(m₁ − m₂)u₁ + 2m₂u₂]/(m₁ + m₂) = [(2 − 3)(5) + 2 × 3 × (−2)]/5 = (−5 − 12)/5 = −3.4 m/s. The 2 kg mass rebounds.

quiz.why: Two forces at 90° form a right triangle, so R = √(8² + 6²) = √100 = 10 N. Adding gives 14 N, which would only be right if they pointed the same way.

quiz.q: Mock 1: Moment of 20 N at 0.5 m
quiz.why: Moment = force × perpendicular distance = 20 × 0.5 = 10 N·m. Multiply the two numbers; do not double or halve.

quiz.q: Mock 1: Centroid of triangle from base (h = 12)
quiz.why: The centroid of a triangle is one-third of the height from the base: 12/3 = 4. From the apex it would be 8.

quiz.q: Mock 1: μ for block just sliding on 30° plane
quiz.why: A block just slides when tan α = μ, so μ = tan 30° = 0.577. The value 0.866 is cos 30°, and 0.5 is sin 30°.

quiz.q: Mock 1: Distance in 5 s from rest at 2 m/s²
quiz.why: Starting from rest, s = ½at² = ½ × 2 × 5² = 25 m. Use t squared, not just t.

quiz.q: Mock 1: KE of 1000 kg at 10 m/s
quiz.why: KE = ½mv² = ½ × 1000 × 10² = 50 000 J = 50 kJ. The speed must be squared before multiplying.

quiz.q: Mock 1: Rod MOI about centre (m = 3 kg, L = 2 m)
quiz.why: For a uniform rod about its centre, I = mL²/12 = 3 × 4/12 = 1 kg·m². The end-axis value mL²/3 would be 4.

quiz.q: Mock 1: Impulse to stop 2 kg at 5 m/s
quiz.why: Impulse equals the change in momentum: the body goes from 2 × 5 = 10 kg·m/s to 0, so the impulse needed is 10 N·s.

questions.q: Unit of moment of a force
questions.why: Moment of a force = force × distance, so its unit is the newton-metre (N·m). W is power, N is force and kg is mass.

questions.q: Equilibrium conditions in 2-D
questions.why: In two dimensions a rigid body needs three conditions: ΣFx = 0, ΣFy = 0 and ΣM = 0. That's three independent equations.

questions.q: Ring MOI
questions.why: All the mass of a ring sits at radius r, so I = mr². A disc has mr²/2 and a solid sphere has 2mr²/5.

questions.q: Coefficient of restitution for perfectly elastic impact
questions.why: For a perfectly elastic impact, the relative speed of separation equals the speed of approach, so e = 1. e = 0 means the bodies stick together.

questions.q: Resultant of 10 N, 10 N, 10 N at 120° to each other
questions.why: Three equal forces at 120° to each other form a closed triangle, so they cancel out. The resultant is 0.

questions.q: Cantilever 2 m with UDL 5 kN/m: fixing moment
questions.why: For a UDL on a cantilever the load is wL = 5 × 2 = 10 kN acting at 1 m, so the moment is wL²/2 = 5 × 4/2 = 10 kN·m.

questions.q: I of 50 × 100 rectangle about base (h = 100)
questions.why: About the base, I = bh³/3 = 50 × 100³/3 = 50 × 10⁶/3 ≈ 1.67×10⁷ mm⁴. The centroidal value bh³/12 is four times smaller (4.17×10⁶).

Force parallel to 45° incline to hold 100 N block, μ = 0.3
questions.why: The block tends to slide down, so friction helps hold it. Force = W sin 45° − μW cos 45° = 100(0.707 − 0.3 × 0.707) = 100(0.707 − 0.212) ≈ 49.5 N.

questions.q: Assertion (A): For an equal-leg angle section, x̄ = ȳ.  Reason (R): The section is symmetric about the line y = x.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: A is true: both legs are equal, so x̄ = ȳ. R is also true, and the symmetry about the line y = x is exactly why the two coordinates are equal. So R explains A.

questions.why: Net force = 3600 − 600 = 3000 N, so a = F/m = 3000/1200 = 2.5 m/s². The resistance must be subtracted first.

Case: A 3 kg ball at 4 m/s hits a 1 kg ball at rest, e = 0.8. Velocity of 1 kg ball after
questions.why: Momentum: 3 × 4 = 3v₁ + v₂ = 12. Restitution: v₂ − v₁ = 0.8 × 4 = 3.2. Substituting gives 4v₁ + 3.2 = 12, so v₁ = 2.2 and v₂ = 5.4 m/s.
