story.title: A drawing that a factory can use

scenes.text: A machinist in another city must make a part from your drawing alone.
Standard lines, lettering and dimensions make the drawing unambiguous.

steps.title: Sheet and lines
steps.body:
Common sheet sizes A0–A4 (A4 = 210 × 297 mm; each larger size doubles the area). Title block at the bottom right.
Line types: thick continuous (visible outlines), thin continuous (dimension, extension, hatching lines), thin short dashes (hidden edges), thin chain (centre lines, axes), thick chain at ends + thin chain (cutting-plane lines), continuous freehand/zigzag (break lines).

steps.title: Dimensioning rules
steps.body:
- Units in mm, unit symbol omitted with a note.
- Each dimension given once; no dimension to a hidden line where avoidable.
- Aligned system (text readable from bottom and right) or unidirectional (all text horizontal).
- Arrowheads ~3:1 length:width; extension lines leave a small gap from the object and extend ~2 mm beyond the dimension line.
- Use Ø for diameter, R for radius; dimension circles in the view where they appear as circles when possible.
- Chain vs parallel (baseline) dimensioning — baseline avoids accumulating errors.

steps.title: Worked examples (described)
steps.body:
**Example 1.** A rectangular plate 80 × 50 with a centred Ø20 hole: draw thick outline, thin centre lines crossing at the hole centre extending 3 mm beyond the circle; dimension 80 and 50 outside the view and Ø20 with a leader.

**Example 2.** A hidden slot in the front view is shown with thin dashed lines; its depth is dimensioned in the side view where it is visible.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Crossing dimension lines and extension lines unnecessarily.
- Using object lines as dimension lines.
- Over-dimensioning (giving the same size twice) or leaving a feature undimensioned.

activity.prompt: Match the line with its use

quiz.why: By drawing convention, hidden edges are shown with thin dashed lines. Thick continuous lines are for visible outlines and thin chain lines for centre lines.
The symbol Ø is used before a number to show a diameter. R is used for radius.
In baseline dimensioning every dimension is measured from one common datum, so errors do not add up from feature to feature. Chain dimensioning builds up cumulative errors.
The ISO A4 sheet is 210 × 297 mm. 297 × 420 is A3 and 148 × 210 is A5.
A dimension should be given once only, in the most suitable view. Repeating it can cause conflicts if one copy is changed or misread.

story.title: Fitting a building on a sheet

scenes.text: A 30 m long building must fit on an A3 sheet.
Draw to scale 1:100 — every 1 cm on paper is 1 m in reality.

steps.title: Representative fraction
steps.body: RF = drawing length/actual length (same units). Reducing scale RF < 1 (1:100), full size 1:1, enlarging RF > 1 (5:1 for small parts). Length of scale L = RF × maximum length to be measured.

steps.title: Plain and diagonal scales
steps.body:
**Plain scale:** reads two units (e.g. m and dm). Divide the scale length into main units; subdivide the first main division into secondary units; zero placed after the first main division.
**Diagonal scale:** reads three units (e.g. m, dm, cm) using the property of similar triangles: draw 10 equal horizontal lines above the scale; diagonals across the first main division let you read 1/10 of the smallest division.

steps.title: Worked examples (described)
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Plain scale RF 1/50 to read metres and decimetres up to 8 m: L = 800 cm/50 = 16 cm. Draw 16 cm, divide into 8 parts of 2 cm (1 m each); subdivide the first part into 10 (1 dm each). Mark 0 at the end of the first part, 1–7 m to the right, dm to the left.

**Example 2.** Diagonal scale RF 1:40 000 to read km, hectometre (0.1 km) and decametre (0.01 km) up to 5 km: L = 500 000 cm/40 000 = 12.5 cm; 5 main divisions of 2.5 cm, first subdivided into 10; 10 horizontal divisions vertically for decametres.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting to convert both lengths to the same unit in RF.
- Placing zero at the extreme left (it goes after the first main division).
- Drawing diagonals in the wrong direction.

activity.prompt: RF = 1/25; maximum length 5 m. Scale length on paper (cm)?

quiz.why: 1 m = 100 cm, so 1 cm on the drawing stands for 100 cm on the object. RF = 1 cm/100 cm = 1/100.
A diagonal scale lets you read three units, for example metres, decimetres and centimetres, using diagonals to subdivide the smallest division.
An enlarging scale makes the drawing bigger than the object, so the representative fraction (drawing/object) is greater than 1.

quiz.q: Zero of a plain scale is placed
quiz.why: On a plain scale the zero is placed after the first main division. The extra division to its left is split into the smaller units.
A diagonal scale works by similar triangles: the diagonals cut the small division into equal proportional parts.

lessons.title: Conic sections by the eccentricity method

scenes.text: Bridge arches are often parabolic; car headlamp reflectors too.
All conics are traced by points whose distance to a focus divided by distance to a directrix is constant — the eccentricity e.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
Conic: locus of a point moving so that (distance from focus F)/(distance from directrix DD) = e.
e < 1 ellipse, e = 1 parabola, e > 1 hyperbola. (Also obtainable by cutting a cone with planes at different angles.)

steps.title: Eccentricity construction (described)
steps.body:
1. Draw directrix DD and the axis perpendicular to it; mark focus F at the given distance.
2. Locate the vertex V on the axis with VF/VC = e (C = foot on directrix), by dividing CF in the ratio.
3. At V erect a perpendicular VE = VF; join C–E and extend — this line gives, for any vertical, the radius e × (distance to directrix).
4. Draw verticals at points 1, 2, 3… on the axis; their heights up to line CE give radii; with F as centre cut each vertical above and below the axis.
5. Join the points with a smooth curve.
**Tangent at a point P:** join PF, draw FT ⊥ PF meeting the directrix at T; TP is the tangent; the normal is perpendicular to it at P.

steps.title: Worked examples (described)
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Ellipse with focus 50 mm from directrix, e = 2/3: divide CF (50) into 5 parts; V is 3 parts from C, i.e. VF = 20 mm, VC = 30 mm; VE = 20 mm. Proceed with steps 3–5.

**Example 2.** Parabola, focus 40 mm from directrix (e = 1): V is midway (20 mm); every point is equidistant from F and DD — use arcs of radius equal to each vertical's distance from DD.

**Example 3.** Other ellipse methods: concentric-circle method (major and minor diameters), oblong (rectangle) method, arcs-of-circles method using the property PF₁ + PF₂ = major axis.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Placing the vertex at the midpoint for e ≠ 1.
- Drawing the curve with a ruler segment instead of a smooth freehand/French-curve line.
- Drawing the tangent perpendicular to PF (it is the line through T and P).

activity.prompt: Which conic?

items.text: Cutting plane parallel to a generator
Plane parallel to the cone axis

quiz.why: For a parabola the distance from the focus equals the distance from the directrix, so the eccentricity e = 1. An ellipse has e < 1 and a hyperbola e > 1.

quiz.q: For e = 3/4, the vertex divides CF so that VF:VC =
quiz.why: Eccentricity e = VF/VC, where C is the foot of the axis on the directrix. For e = 3/4, VF : VC = 3 : 4.

quiz.q: Sum of focal distances is constant for
quiz.why: An ellipse is the curve for which the sum of the distances from the two foci is constant. For a hyperbola the difference is constant.
A parabolic reflector sends light from the focus out as a parallel beam, which is why headlamps use it.

quiz.q: Tangent construction uses a line FT
quiz.why: To draw the tangent, join P to the focus F, then draw a line from F perpendicular to PF to meet the directrix at T. Joining T to P gives the tangent.

scenes.text: Most gear teeth have involute profiles so they mesh smoothly.
A point on a rolling wheel traces a cycloid — the curve behind early clock gears.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
- **Cycloid:** locus of a point on a circle rolling without slipping along a straight line. Length of base = πD.
- **Epicycloid / hypocycloid:** circle rolling outside / inside another circle.
- **Involute:** locus of the end of a taut string unwound from a circle (or polygon). For a circle, the string length after one turn = πD.

steps.title: Construction (described)
steps.body:
**Cycloid:** draw the circle (diameter D) on the base line; base length πD divided into 12 equal parts; divide the circle into 12; draw the locus of centres (line at height D/2), mark C₁…C₁₂; from each circle division draw horizontal lines; with radius D/2 and centre Cₙ cut the nth horizontal line; join points smoothly.
**Involute of a circle:** divide circle into 12; at each point draw a tangent; along the nth tangent mark length n × πD/12; join the ends.
Normal to a cycloid at P: from P with radius D/2 cut the locus of centres at C, drop to the base at N; PN is normal, tangent ⊥ PN. Normal to an involute at P is the tangent from P to the circle.

steps.title: Worked examples (described)
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Rolling circle D = 50 mm: base length = π × 50 = 157 mm; each of 12 divisions = 13.1 mm.

**Example 2.** Involute of a 40 mm circle: final string length = 125.7 mm; along tangent 6 mark 62.8 mm.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Base length taken as D instead of πD.
- Drawing tangents to the circle in the wrong direction for the involute.
- Joining points with straight segments.

activity.prompt: Cycloid base length for a rolling circle of diameter 60 mm (mm, 1 decimal)

quiz.why: A cycloid is generated by a circle rolling for one revolution along a line, so the base length equals the circumference, πD.
An involute is the path traced by the end of a taut string as it is unwound from a circle. A rolling circle makes a cycloid.
options: end of a string unwound from a circle

quiz.q: Circle rolling outside another circle traces
quiz.why: A circle rolling on the outside of another circle traces an epicycloid. Rolling on the inside gives a hypocycloid.

quiz.q: Normal to an involute at P is
quiz.why: The string is always tangent to the base circle, so the normal to an involute at P is the tangent from P to the base circle.
options: tangent from P to the base circle

quiz.why: The involute is the standard gear tooth profile, because meshing gears with this shape keep a constant speed ratio and tolerate small centre-distance changes.

questions.q: Line for centre lines
questions.why: By convention centre lines are drawn as thin chain lines (long and short dashes). Dashed lines mean hidden edges.

questions.q: RF 1:1 is
questions.why: An RF of 1:1 means the drawing is the same size as the object. It's the full-size scale.

questions.q: Eccentricity of ellipse
questions.why: An ellipse has eccentricity e < 1 (the focus is nearer than the directrix distance ratio). Parabola is 1 and hyperbola is above 1.

questions.q: RF for 1 cm representing 5 m
questions.why: 5 m = 500 cm, so 1 cm represents 500 cm. RF = 1/500.

questions.q: Unidirectional dimensioning places text
questions.why: In the unidirectional system all dimension text is horizontal, so the sheet can be read from the bottom. The aligned system turns text along dimension lines.

questions.q: Scale length for RF 1/40, max 6 m
questions.why: Scale length = RF × maximum length = 600 cm/40 = 15 cm.

questions.q: Assertion (A): A diagonal scale can measure three units.  Reason (R): Its diagonals divide the smallest main sub-division into ten parts by similar triangles.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: A is true: a diagonal scale reads three units. R is true and explains it: the diagonals divide the smallest sub-division into ten parts by similar triangles.

questions.q: Focus 60 mm from directrix, e = 1/2 (ellipse): VF
questions.why: With e = VF/VC = 1/2 and CF = VF + VC = 60, VF = 60 × (1/2)/(1 + 1/2) = 20 mm.

questions.q: Involute string length after one turn, D = 35 mm
questions.why: After one full turn the string unwound equals the circumference: π × 35 ≈ 110 mm.

questions.q: Parabola: focus 50 mm from directrix — vertex distance from focus
questions.why: The vertex of a parabola is midway between the focus and the directrix, so VF = 50/2 = 25 mm.

questions.q: Case: A map uses RF 1/50 000 and you need to read 0.1 km (hectometres) and km up to 8 km. Scale length
questions.why: The scale must cover 8 km = 800 000 cm. Length = 800 000/50 000 = 16 cm.

questions.q: Hyperbola with e = 3/2, focus 50 mm from directrix: VF
questions.why: For a hyperbola VF/VC = e = 3/2, and VF + VC = 50 gives VF = (3/5) × 50 = 30 mm.

questions.q: Each of 12 divisions of a cycloid base for D = 42 mm
questions.why: The base of one cycloid revolution is πD = π × 42 ≈ 132 mm. Divided into 12 equal parts, each is about 11 mm.

questions.q: The normal to a cycloid at P passes through
questions.why: The rolling circle is instantly turning about its point of contact with the base line, so the normal to the cycloid at P passes through that contact point.
options: the point of contact of the rolling circle with the base at that instant
the centre of the rolling circle

questions.q: Sizes: A0 area is
questions.why: A0 is defined to have an area of 1 m² (841 × 1189 mm). Each next size halves the area.

courses.title: Engineering Graphics · Unit 2 · Orthographic projections of points, lines and planes
courses.summary: First- and third-angle projection, reference planes and quadrants, projections of points, lines parallel/inclined to planes, true length and true inclinations, traces, and projections of plane laminas — described step by step.
outcomes: Explain first- and third-angle projection and their symbols
Project points in all four quadrants
Find true length and inclinations of lines (rotation and auxiliary methods)
Project plane figures inclined to one or both reference planes
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

scenes.text: A part designed in India is made by a supplier abroad.
Is the side view on the left or right? It depends on first- vs third-angle convention.

steps.title: Reference planes and views
steps.body: Vertical plane (VP) and horizontal plane (HP) intersect along XY, forming four quadrants. Front view (elevation) on VP, top view (plan) on HP, side view on profile plane (PP). Projectors are perpendicular to the planes (parallel projection).

steps.title: First vs third angle
steps.body:
**First angle (object in 1st quadrant):** object between observer and plane. Top view below the front view; left-side view drawn to the right of the front view. Used in India (BIS SP 46) and much of Europe.
**Third angle:** plane between observer and object. Top view above the front view; right-side view to the right. Common in the USA.
Symbol: truncated cone views — learn which way the circles sit for each method.

steps.title: Worked examples (described)
steps.body:
**Example 1.** A step block viewed from the front (arrow) in first angle: draw the front view above XY; project downwards for the top view; project horizontally to the right for the left-side view.

**Example 2.** The same block in third angle: top view above the front view; right-side view to the right.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing first- and third-angle placement on one sheet.
- Drawing the side view without projecting from both front and top views.
- Forgetting hidden lines.

activity.prompt: Which projection method?

items.text: Top view placed below the front view
Top view placed above the front view
Left-side view placed to the right of the front view
Right-side view placed to the right of the front view

quiz.why: The front view is projected on the vertical plane (VP). The top view goes on the horizontal plane (HP).

quiz.q: In first angle the top view is
quiz.why: In first-angle projection the object lies between the observer and the plane, so the top view is placed below XY, below the front view.
The BIS (SP 46) recommends first-angle projection for engineering drawings in India, so that is used here.
In orthographic projection the projectors are parallel to each other and perpendicular to the plane of projection. Converging projectors are used in perspective.
options: parallel and perpendicular to the plane

quiz.why: XY is the reference line where the vertical plane and the horizontal plane intersect.

scenes.text: A sensor sits 20 mm above HP and 30 mm in front of VP.
Its front and top views are fixed by those two distances.

steps.title: Rules
steps.body:
Point P: front view p′, top view p, on the same projector perpendicular to XY.
- Distance of p′ from XY = height above (or below) HP.
- Distance of p from XY = distance in front of (or behind) VP.
Quadrant placement (after rotating HP): 1st — p′ above, p below XY; 2nd — both above; 3rd — p′ below, p above; 4th — both below.

steps.title: Worked examples (described)
steps.body:
**Example 1.** A: 20 mm above HP, 30 mm in front of VP (1st quadrant): a′ 20 mm above XY; a 30 mm below XY.

**Example 2.** B: 25 mm above HP, 15 mm behind VP (2nd quadrant): b′ 25 above, b 15 above XY.

**Example 3.** C on HP, 20 mm in front of VP: c′ on XY; c 20 mm below XY.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Placing the top view above XY for a point in front of VP (that's 2nd/3rd quadrant).
- Not keeping both views on one projector.
- Confusing 'behind VP' with 'below HP'.

activity.prompt: Point position → view placement (first-angle layout)

quiz.q: Distance of FV from XY gives
quiz.why: The distance of the front view from XY shows how high the point is above HP. The top view's distance from XY gives the distance from VP.

quiz.q: Both views above XY means the point is in
quiz.why: A point whose front and top views are both above XY lies above HP and behind VP, which is the second quadrant.

quiz.q: A point on HP has its front view
quiz.why: A point on HP has zero height, so its front view is at zero distance above XY, that is on XY.

quiz.q: Front and top views of a point lie on
quiz.why: The front and top views of a point lie on the same projector, which is a line perpendicular to XY.

quiz.q: Point 10 mm below HP, 20 mm behind VP lies in
quiz.why: Below HP and behind VP puts the point in the third quadrant. The first is above HP and in front of VP.

lessons.title: Projections of straight lines and true length

scenes.text: A pipe runs from a pump to a tank at some angle to both the floor and the wall.
Its views look shorter than it is — we need its true length and angles to cut it.

steps.title: Cases
steps.body:
- Line parallel to both planes: both views true length (TL).
- Parallel to VP, inclined θ to HP: FV = TL at θ to XY; TV parallel to XY (shortened).
- Parallel to HP, inclined φ to VP: TV = TL at φ; FV parallel to XY.
- Inclined to both: neither view is TL; apparent angles α (FV) > θ and β (TV) > φ.

steps.title: Finding TL and true inclinations (rotating-line method, described)
steps.body:
1. Draw the given FV a′b′ and TV ab.
2. Rotate TV ab about a until parallel to XY (ab₁); project b₁ up to the locus of b′ ⇒ a′b₁′ = TL and its angle with XY = θ (inclination to HP).
3. Rotate FV a′b′ about a′ until parallel to XY; project down to the locus of b ⇒ ab₂ = TL, angle with XY = φ (inclination to VP).
**Traces:** HT = point where the line (extended) meets HP; VT where it meets VP.
Alternative: auxiliary plane method (project onto a plane parallel to the line).

steps.title: Worked examples (described)
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Line AB 80 mm, parallel to VP, inclined 30° to HP; A 10 mm above HP, 20 mm in front of VP: draw a′b′ = 80 at 30°; TV ab parallel to XY, 20 below XY, length 80 cos 30° = 69.3 mm.

**Example 2.** A line's TV is 50 mm long and its ends differ in height by 30 mm: rotating the TV parallel to XY and projecting gives TL = √(50² + 30²) ≈ 58.3 mm and θ = tan⁻¹(30/50) ≈ 31°.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Measuring true angles from apparent views.
- Rotating about the wrong end or not keeping the end's locus.
- Forgetting that TL is always ≥ both projections.

activity.prompt: Line 100 mm parallel to VP, inclined 60° to HP. Length of its top view (mm)?

quiz.q: A line parallel to VP shows true length in
quiz.why: A line parallel to the VP is seen at its true length in the front view, because the front view is on the VP.

quiz.q: Apparent angle in FV compared with θ
quiz.why: For a line inclined to both planes the apparent angle in a view is greater than the true inclination, since the projected length shrinks while the height stays the same.

quiz.q: HT is where the line meets
quiz.why: The horizontal trace (HT) is the point where the line, extended, meets the horizontal plane (HP).
The true length is found by rotating a view until it is parallel to XY (or by a trapezoid method), because a line parallel to a plane shows its true length there.
options: rotating a view parallel to XY

quiz.q: Top view length of line inclined θ to HP and parallel to VP
quiz.why: A line parallel to VP and inclined θ to HP has a top view of L cos θ, since the horizontal projection of the length along the incline is L cos θ.

scenes.text: A triangular gusset plate is welded at an angle in a frame.
Its true shape appears only in the view where it is parallel to a plane.

steps.title: Approach (change of position)
steps.body:
Step 1: assume the plane parallel to HP (true shape in TV) with one edge perpendicular/parallel to VP as needed.
Step 2: tilt it to the given angle θ with HP — FV becomes an edge view (line) at θ; project the TV.
Step 3: rotate the TV so the edge/diagonal makes the given angle with VP; project the final FV.
Plane perpendicular to both planes: both views are lines.

steps.title: Worked examples (described)
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Square 40 mm side, surface inclined 30° to HP, one side on HP and perpendicular to VP: Step 1 true square in TV; Step 2 FV is a 40 mm line at 30° to XY; TV becomes a rectangle 40 × 34.6 mm.

**Example 2.** Regular hexagon 30 mm side resting on a corner with surface 45° to HP and the diagonal through that corner inclined 30° to VP: three stages as above; final views are irregular hexagons.

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Lengths of edges parallel to the plane of rotation stay unchanged — use them to check each stage.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Attempting the final position directly without the intermediate stages.
- Mixing up 'surface inclined to HP' with 'edge inclined to HP'.
- Drawing hidden lines for a lamina of negligible thickness (not needed).

activity.prompt: Stages for a plane inclined to both reference planes
items: Draw the true shape in the view where it is parallel to a reference plane
Tilt to the given angle with HP: draw the edge view and project
Rotate the new top view to the given angle with VP
Project the final front view
Darken the final views and label corners

quiz.q: True shape of a plane appears in the view
quiz.why: The true shape of a plane figure appears in the view on a plane parallel to the figure.

quiz.q: A plane perpendicular to VP and inclined to HP: FV is
quiz.why: A plane perpendicular to VP and inclined to HP appears in the front view as a line (an edge view) inclined to XY at that same angle.

quiz.q: Square 40 mm inclined 60° to HP (edge on HP ⊥ VP): TV width along tilt
quiz.why: With the edge on HP and the square tilted 60°, the width of the top view along the tilt is 40 cos 60° = 20 mm.

quiz.q: Number of stages for planes inclined to both planes
quiz.why: Planes inclined to both planes are usually drawn in three stages: first a simple position, then a tilt to one plane, then a tilt to the other.

quiz.q: Thickness of a plane lamina is
quiz.why: A lamina is a plane figure of negligible thickness, so its thickness is neglected in the drawing.

questions.q: Top view is projected on
questions.why: The top view (plan) is projected on the horizontal plane, HP.

questions.q: BIS SP 46 is a code for
questions.why: BIS SP 46 is the Bureau of Indian Standards code of practice for engineering drawing.

questions.q: Point in 1st quadrant: TV lies
questions.why: A point in the first quadrant is above HP and in front of VP. After the planes are opened, its top view lies below XY.

questions.q: Line perpendicular to HP: TV is
questions.why: A line perpendicular to HP is seen end-on from above, so its top view is a point.

questions.q: Line parallel to HP, 70 mm, 30° to VP: FV length
questions.why: A line parallel to HP shows its true length in the top view. Its front view is shortened to 70 cos 30° ≈ 60.6 mm.

questions.q: Point 15 mm above HP, 25 mm behind VP: positions
questions.why: Above HP puts the front view 15 mm above XY. Behind VP means that after rotation the top view is above XY too, at 25 mm.
options: FV 15 above XY, TV 25 above XY

questions.q: Assertion (A): For a line inclined to both HP and VP, neither projection shows the true length.  Reason (R): Each projection is foreshortened by the inclination to the respective plane.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: A is true: when the line is inclined to both planes, both views are shorter than the true length. R is true and explains it, since each projection is shortened by its inclination, so the true length has to be constructed.

questions.q: A line parallel to VP has ends 20 mm and 60 mm above HP and true length 50 mm. Its inclination θ to HP
questions.why: The height difference is 60 − 20 = 40 mm and the true length is 50 mm. sin θ = 40/50 = 0.8, so θ ≈ 53.1°.

questions.q: Third-angle projection places the right-side view
questions.why: In third-angle projection the right-side view is placed to the right of the front view. The top view goes above the front view.
options: to the right of the front view

questions.q: Hexagon of 25 mm side parallel to HP: TV shows
questions.why: A hexagon parallel to HP is seen undistorted from above, so its top view shows its true shape.

questions.q: Case: A 60 mm pipe is parallel to VP and rises 30 mm from one end to the other. Its inclination to HP
questions.why: The pipe is parallel to VP, so the front view shows its true length. The rise is 30 mm on a 60 mm pipe, so sin θ = 30/60 = 0.5 and θ = 30°.

questions.q: Circle of 50 mm diameter, surface inclined 30° to HP: TV is
questions.why: A circle inclined 30° to HP projects as an ellipse. Its major axis stays 50 mm and its minor axis shrinks to 50 cos 30° = 43.3 mm.

questions.q: A line's FV is parallel to XY. The line is
questions.why: If the front view is parallel to XY, the heights of the two ends are equal, so the line is parallel to HP.

questions.q: TL from a top view 50 mm long with end heights differing by 30 mm (rotate the TV): TL
questions.why: The true length is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with sides 50 and 30: √(2500 + 900) = √3400 ≈ 58.3 mm.

questions.q: VT of a line lies
questions.why: The vertical trace (VT) is where the line meets VP. It lies on the front view, extended if needed, at the point where the line crosses VP.

courses.title: Engineering Graphics · Unit 3 · Projections of solids, sections and development of surfaces
courses.summary: Classification of solids, projections of prisms, pyramids, cylinders and cones in simple and inclined positions, sectional views and true shape of sections, and development of lateral surfaces — described step by step.
outcomes: Project prisms, pyramids, cylinders and cones with axis perpendicular or inclined
Draw sectional views and the true shape of a section
Develop lateral surfaces by parallel-line and radial-line methods
Apply sections and developments to sheet-metal problems
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

scenes.text: A designer sketches a hexagonal gift box (prism) and a conical cup.
Their orthographic views start from the base shape.

steps.title: Classification
steps.body: Polyhedra: prisms and pyramids (named by base: triangular, square, pentagonal, hexagonal), tetrahedron, cube. Solids of revolution: cylinder, cone, sphere. Frustum = part between base and a cutting plane parallel to it; truncated = cut by an inclined plane.

steps.title: Axis perpendicular to HP (resting on base)
steps.body: TV shows the true base shape; FV is a rectangle (prism/cylinder) or triangle (pyramid/cone) of height h. Axis perpendicular to VP: FV shows the true base. Axis parallel to both: side view shows the base.

steps.title: Worked examples (described)
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Hexagonal prism, base side 25, axis 50, resting on HP with two base edges parallel to VP: TV a regular hexagon with two horizontal sides; FV a 50 mm tall rectangle 50 mm wide (corner-to-corner = 2 × 25) with two inner vertical lines for the visible edges.

**Example 2.** Cone, base Ø40, axis 60, base on HP: TV a circle with the apex at the centre; FV an isosceles triangle 40 wide and 60 high.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Wrong orientation of base edges (parallel vs perpendicular to VP).
- Omitting edges that are visible in the FV.
- Drawing a hidden line where an edge is actually visible.

activity.prompt: Solid → front view when resting on its base on HP

quiz.q: Base shape appears true in TV when
quiz.why: If the axis is perpendicular to HP, the base is parallel to HP and so its true shape appears in the top view.
A frustum is the part of a cone (or pyramid) between its base and a cut plane parallel to the base.
options: the part between base and a parallel cut
a cone cut along its axis

quiz.q: FV of a cylinder with axis ⊥ VP
quiz.why: If the axis of a cylinder is perpendicular to VP, you look at it end-on in the front view, so the front view is a circle.
A cube is a prism with a square base whose height equals the base edge, so all edges are equal.

quiz.q: Width of FV of hexagonal prism (corners left–right), side 30
quiz.why: A regular hexagon with corners left–right measures twice its side corner to corner, so the width is 2 × 30 = 60 mm.

story.title: A tilted cone in a hopper

scenes.text: A grain hopper is a cone tilted on its stand.
Draw it in a simple position first, then tilt it — the two-stage method.

steps.title: Two-stage (change of position) method
steps.body:
Stage 1: draw the solid with axis perpendicular to the plane to which it will be inclined (e.g. axis ⊥ HP).
Stage 2: tilt the FV so the axis makes θ with HP (or the base/edge/face rests as specified), keeping lengths; project the new TV from the old TV (same widths along projectors).
Stage 3 (if inclined to VP too): rotate the TV to make the axis' plan at the given angle; project the final FV.

steps.title: Worked examples (described)
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Square pyramid base 40, axis 60, resting on a base edge on HP with axis inclined 30° to HP and parallel to VP: Stage 1 axis ⊥ HP with the resting edge ⊥ VP; Stage 2 tilt the triangular FV about the resting edge until the axis is at 30° to XY... equivalently the base makes 60° with HP; project the TV.

**Example 2.** Cylinder Ø50, axis 70, resting on a generator on HP with axis inclined 45° to VP: Stage 1 axis ⊥ VP (FV circle); Stage 2 rotate TV rectangle to 45°; project FV (ellipses at the ends).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Tilting the wrong view (tilt the view where the axis appears as a line).
- Confusing 'axis inclined at θ' with 'base inclined at θ' (they are complementary for a right solid).
- Not projecting widths faithfully from the previous stage.

activity.prompt: Projecting a solid inclined to HP and VP
items: Draw the solid with axis perpendicular to HP (simple position)
Tilt the front view to the required angle with HP
Project the new top view
Rotate the top view to the required angle with VP
Project the final front view and mark hidden edges

quiz.q: If the axis makes 30° with HP, the base makes
quiz.why: For a right solid the base is perpendicular to the axis, so if the axis makes 30° with HP, the base makes 90° − 30° = 60° with HP.
In the first (simple) position, the axis is perpendicular to one of the reference planes, so the views are easy to draw.

quiz.q: Base circle of a tilted cylinder appears as
quiz.why: A circular base tilted to the viewing plane is seen as an ellipse, because it is foreshortened in one direction only.

quiz.q: Lengths unchanged when tilting are those
quiz.why: When a solid is tilted, lengths lying in the plane of rotation keep their size in the view parallel to that plane.
A finished view needs visible edges drawn as thick continuous lines and hidden edges as dashed lines, so the shape can be read correctly.

lessons.title: Sections of solids and true shape

scenes.text: An engineer needs to see the inside of a hollow casting.
A sectional view cuts it with an imaginary plane and hatches the cut surface.

steps.title: Section planes
steps.body:
Section plane shown by its trace (cutting-plane line) in the view where it appears as a line. Parts between the observer and plane are removed. Cut surfaces are hatched with thin lines at 45° (closely spaced, uniform).
Section plane perpendicular to VP, inclined to HP: FV shows it as a line; the sectional TV is drawn; the **true shape** is obtained on an auxiliary plane parallel to the section plane (projectors perpendicular to the cutting-plane line, widths transferred from the TV).

steps.title: Shapes of sections
steps.body:
Cone: plane through apex — triangle; parallel to base — circle; inclined cutting all generators — ellipse; parallel to a generator — parabola; parallel to axis (not through it) — hyperbola.
Cylinder: parallel to axis — rectangle; inclined — ellipse.

steps.title: Worked examples (described)
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Square pyramid base 40, axis 60, cut by a plane ⊥ VP inclined 30° to HP bisecting the axis: mark the cutting line in FV through the midpoint of the axis; find where it cuts each slant edge; project those points to the TV; hatch the section; draw the true shape (quadrilateral) on an auxiliary XY parallel to the cutting line.

**Example 2.** Cylinder Ø50 cut at 45° to its axis: true shape is an ellipse with minor axis 50 and major axis 50/sin 45° = 70.7 mm.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Hatching the uncut surfaces.
- Taking widths for the true shape from the FV instead of the TV.
- Forgetting that a plane through the apex of a cone gives a triangle.

activity.prompt: Section of a right circular cone

items.text: Plane through the apex and base

quiz.why: Section hatching lines are normally drawn at 45° to the main outline. This helps the reader see the cut surfaces.

quiz.q: True shape of a section is seen on a plane
quiz.why: The true shape of a section is seen in an auxiliary view on a plane parallel to the cutting plane, because only then is it undistorted.

quiz.q: Cylinder cut parallel to its axis gives
quiz.why: A plane parallel to the axis of a cylinder cuts along two straight generators, so the section is a rectangle.

quiz.q: Cylinder Ø40 cut at 30° to its axis: major axis of ellipse
quiz.why: The major axis of the elliptical section is D/sin θ = 40/sin 30° = 80 mm, where θ is the angle of the plane with the axis.
The cutting plane line is drawn as a thin chain line, thick at its ends and at changes of direction, with arrows showing the viewing direction.
options: thin chain, thick at ends with arrows

scenes.text: A sheet-metal worker must cut a flat pattern that rolls into a conical funnel.
That flat pattern is the development of the surface.

steps.title: Methods
steps.body:
**Parallel-line method:** prisms and cylinders. Lateral surface unrolls into a rectangle: width = perimeter (πD for a cylinder), height = axis length. Divide into equal parts (12 for a cylinder), project cut points horizontally to their generators.
**Radial-line method:** pyramids and cones. Cone development is a sector of radius = slant height L and angle θ = 360° × r/L. Pyramids: triangles of slant edge length laid around a centre.
**Triangulation:** transition pieces (e.g. square-to-round).

steps.title: Worked examples (described)
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Cone base Ø60, height 40: L = √(30² + 40²) = 50; θ = 360 × 30/50 = 216°. Draw an arc of radius 50 subtending 216°; divide into 12; join to the centre.

**Example 2.** Cylinder Ø40, height 60, cut by a 45° plane through the axis midpoint: development is a 125.7 × 60 rectangle; mark the cut heights on the 12 generators and join with a smooth sine-like curve.

**Example 3.** Square prism side 30, height 50: development is a 120 × 50 rectangle divided into four 30-wide faces.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the vertical height instead of slant height for a cone's radius.
- Taking true lengths of pyramid slant edges from a view where they are foreshortened.
- Joining cut points with straight lines on a cylinder development (it should be a smooth curve).

activity.prompt: Cone: base radius 35 mm, slant height 70 mm. Sector angle of development (degrees)?

quiz.q: Development of a cylinder's lateral surface
quiz.why: Unrolling the curved surface of a cylinder gives a rectangle whose length is the circumference πD and whose width is the height h.
A cone's curved surface develops into a sector of a circle whose radius equals the slant height.
The arc of the sector equals the base circumference 2πr, so θ/360° = 2πr/(2πL), giving θ = 360° × r/L.
The parallel-line method fits prisms and cylinders, whose edges (generators) are all parallel. Cones use the radial-line method.

questions.q: A prism with a hexagonal base has lateral faces
questions.why: A prism has one rectangular lateral face for each edge of its base, so a hexagonal prism has 6.

questions.q: Section lines (hatching) indicate
questions.why: Hatching shows the surfaces that were cut by the section plane, so they stand apart from the uncut surfaces behind.

questions.q: Cylinder development width
questions.why: The cylinder's lateral surface unrolls into a rectangle whose width is the circumference, πD.

questions.q: Cone base Ø50, height 60: slant height
questions.why: Radius = 25 mm and height = 60 mm, so L = √(25² + 60²) = √(625 + 3600) = √4225 = 65 mm.

questions.q: Sector angle for that cone
Sphere cut by any plane gives
questions.why: Every plane section of a sphere is a circle, wherever and however the plane cuts it.

questions.q: Assertion (A): The true shape of an inclined section is not seen in the front or top view.  Reason (R): The section plane is inclined to both those planes' parallels — only an auxiliary view parallel to it shows true size.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: A is true: an inclined section is not parallel to the principal planes, so it is foreshortened in the front and top views. R is true and explains it, because the true size appears only in an auxiliary view parallel to the section.

questions.q: Cone cut by a plane parallel to its axis (not through apex)
questions.why: A plane parallel to the axis of a cone (but not through the apex) cuts both nappes of the geometric cone, giving a hyperbola. A plane parallel to a generator gives a parabola.

questions.q: Development of a square pyramid's lateral surface consists of
questions.why: A square pyramid has four triangular faces. When developed they form four triangles joined around the apex point.

questions.q: Square prism side 25, height 60: development size
questions.why: The development is a rectangle whose length is the base perimeter 4 × 25 = 100 mm and whose height is 60 mm.

questions.q: Case: A chimney cap is a cone of base Ø80 and slant height 80 mm. Sector angle
questions.why: θ = 360° × r/L = 360° × 40/80 = 180°, so the development is a semicircle.

questions.q: Cylinder Ø60 cut at 60° to its axis: major axis of section
questions.why: The major axis is D/sin θ = 60/sin 60° = 60/0.866 ≈ 69.3 mm.

questions.q: When a square pyramid rests on a base edge with base at 45° to HP, its axis makes
questions.why: The axis of a right pyramid is perpendicular to its base. If the base is at 45° to HP, the axis is at 90° − 45° = 45° to HP.

questions.q: Transition pieces (square-to-round) are developed by
questions.why: A transition piece joins different shapes (square to round), so its surface is split into triangles and developed by triangulation.

questions.q: Hexagonal pyramid edge true length is found by
questions.why: A slant edge shows its true length only when it is parallel to a plane. Rotating the edge until it is parallel to VP gives its true length in the front view.
options: rotating the slant edge to be parallel to VP

courses.title: Engineering Graphics · Unit 4 · Isometric projection, reading drawings and CAD basics
courses.summary: Isometric scale and isometric views, isometric drawing of solids and simple machine parts, converting pictorial views to orthographic and vice versa, and an introduction to 2-D CAD workflow (commands, layers, dimensioning, printing).
outcomes: Construct an isometric scale and isometric views
Draw isometric views of solids and blocks with circles (four-centre method)
Convert between pictorial and orthographic views
Produce a clean 2-D CAD drawing with layers and dimensions
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

scenes.text: Flat-pack furniture manuals show parts in a 3-D-looking view.
These are isometric drawings — three axes 120° apart.

steps.title: Isometric projection vs drawing
steps.body:
Isometric axes at 120° to each other (one vertical, two at 30° to the horizontal). In **isometric projection**, lengths along the axes are reduced to 0.816 (√(2/3)) of true length using an isometric scale. In **isometric drawing** (view), true lengths are used — larger but easier; commonly used in exams unless 'projection' is asked.
Lines parallel to the axes are isometric lines (measured); non-isometric lines are drawn by locating their end points.

steps.title: Isometric scale (described)
steps.body: Draw a horizontal line; from one end draw a line at 45° (true scale) and another at 30° (isometric scale). Mark true divisions on the 45° line; drop verticals to the 30° line — the intercepts are isometric lengths (ratio cos 45°/cos 30° = 0.816).

steps.title: Worked examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** A 50 mm edge in isometric projection measures 50 × 0.816 = 40.8 mm.

steps.title: Box method and circles
steps.body:
Enclose the solid in a box (isometric rectangle prism), locate features on the box faces, then remove construction lines.
**Four-centre method for an isometric circle:** draw the isometric square (rhombus) of side = diameter; from the two obtuse corners draw lines to the midpoints of the opposite sides; their intersections give two more centres; draw four arcs (two large, two small) to form the ellipse.

steps.title: Worked examples (described)
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Cylinder Ø40, height 50, axis vertical: rhombus 40 × 40 on the top face; four-centre ellipse; repeat at the bottom (or offset centres down 50); join with vertical tangents.

**Example 2.** Square pyramid base 40, height 60: draw the base rhombus; locate the centre; erect 60 mm vertical; join apex to the four corners (slant edges are non-isometric).

**Example 3.** Sphere: in isometric projection its outline is a circle of the true radius (its centre is located with the isometric scale); in an isometric drawing, where all lengths are 1.22 times larger, the circle is drawn with radius 1.22R.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Drawing the isometric circle as a true circle.
- Wrong plane orientation of the rhombus (top, front or side face).
- Leaving construction lines dark.

quiz.why: A circle in isometric view is not parallel to the viewing plane, so it appears as an ellipse.
The four-centre method draws an isometric rhombus whose side equals the circle's diameter, then draws arcs from four centres to give an approximate ellipse.

quiz.q: Slant edges of a pyramid in isometric are
quiz.why: Slant edges of a pyramid are not parallel to any isometric axis, so they are non-isometric lines and must be found by locating their ends.

quiz.q: Box method encloses the solid in
quiz.why: In the box method an isometric box encloses the object, and the features are located inside it.

quiz.q: Construction lines in final drawing should be
quiz.why: Construction lines should be drawn light or erased, so they do not confuse the final outlines.

steps.title: Pictorial → orthographic
steps.body: Choose the front view direction (most informative, fewest hidden lines). Project the FV, TV and side view in first angle with correct alignment: FV and TV share widths; FV and SV share heights; TV and SV share depths (use a 45° mitre line). Show hidden edges dashed and centre lines for holes.

steps.title: Orthographic → isometric
steps.body: Box the overall dimensions; transfer each feature using coordinates from the views; check each surface: a surface seen as a line in one view and an area in another is perpendicular to the first plane; an inclined surface appears as a line in one view and similar-shaped areas in the other two.

steps.title: Worked examples (described)
steps.body:
**Example 1.** L-shaped bracket with a hole: FV shows the L; TV shows the base with a circle (hole) and centre lines; SV shows the vertical leg as a rectangle with hidden lines for the hole.

**Example 2.** From views showing a sloped face as a line in FV and a rectangle in TV and SV, the face is perpendicular to VP and inclined to HP — draw it in isometric by locating its corner points.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Misaligned views (sizes not projected).
- Missing hidden lines or centre lines.
- Choosing a front view with many hidden lines.

quiz.why: The front view and the top view are one above the other, so they share the same width and line up vertically.
A 45° mitre line carries the depth measurement from the top view across to the side view.
The best front view shows the most detail with the fewest hidden lines, so it is easiest to read.

quiz.q: A surface appearing as a line in FV is
quiz.why: A surface that looks like a line in the front view is seen edge-on, so it is perpendicular to VP.
Holes need centre lines (thin chain lines) in views to mark their axes and centres.

scenes.text: In industry, drawings are made in CAD software and shared as files.

steps.title: Workflow (generic, applies to most 2-D CAD tools)
steps.body:
1. Set units (mm), limits and a drawing template with title block.
2. Create **layers** for object, hidden, centre, dimension, hatch, text — each with its line type and weight.
3. Draw with precise input: absolute (x,y), relative (@dx,dy), polar (@length<angle); use object snaps (endpoint, midpoint, centre, intersection, perpendicular, tangent) and ortho/polar tracking.
4. Edit: trim, extend, offset, fillet, chamfer, mirror, array, move, copy, rotate, scale.
5. Annotate: dimension styles (text height, arrow size), hatching, text.
6. Plot/print to scale; export to PDF.

steps.title: Worked examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Draw a 100 × 60 rectangle starting at (0,0): line to @100,0, @0,60, @−100,0, close.

**Example 2.** A Ø20 hole at the centre: circle with centre at (50,30), diameter 20; centre lines on the centre layer.

**Example 3.** Six holes on a PCD Ø80: draw one hole, then a polar array of 6 about the centre.

steps.title: Good CAD habits
steps.body: Draw at full size (1:1) in model space and scale only when plotting; keep one feature type per layer; save versions frequently.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Drawing everything on one layer.
- Ignoring snaps and typing approximate values.
- Exploding dimensions (they stop updating with geometry).

quiz.q: Relative coordinate input for 50 mm right
quiz.why: In CAD, the @ sign means relative to the last point. @50,0 means 50 units along x and 0 along y, which is 50 mm to the right.
Relative polar input is written @length<angle, so 40 mm at 30° is @40<30. The order is length first, then angle.

quiz.q: Command to create evenly spaced copies around a centre
quiz.why: A polar array makes evenly spaced copies of an object around a centre point.
Layers organise a drawing by line type, colour and kind of object, so groups such as hidden lines or dimensions can be controlled together.

quiz.q: Recommended drawing scale in model space
quiz.why: Draw at full size (1:1) in model space, and set the scale only when plotting. This keeps dimensions true.

questions.q: Isometric axes are
questions.why: The isometric axes are 120° apart from one another. The name means equal measure, since the three axes are equally foreshortened.

questions.q: CAD command to make a parallel copy at a distance
questions.why: The OFFSET command makes a parallel copy of a line or curve at a given distance.

questions.q: Isometric circle drawn by
questions.why: An isometric circle is drawn with the four-centre method, which gives an approximate ellipse using four arcs.

questions.q: 100 mm edge in isometric projection
questions.why: In isometric projection lengths are shortened by 0.816, so 100 mm becomes about 81.6 mm. Isometric drawing keeps 100 mm.

questions.q: Front and side views share
questions.why: The front view and the side view are side by side, so they share the same height.

questions.q: CAD snap for the centre of a circle
questions.why: To pick the centre of a circle or arc in CAD, use the Centre object snap.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Isometric drawings are larger than isometric projections.  Reason (R): Isometric drawings use true lengths instead of the 0.816 isometric scale.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: A is true: an isometric drawing is larger than the projection. R is true and explains it, because the drawing uses true lengths while the projection uses the 0.816 scale.

questions.q: Sloping face seen as a line in FV is
questions.why: A face seen as a sloping line in the front view is perpendicular to VP, so it appears edge-on, and it is inclined to HP.
options: perpendicular to VP, inclined to HP

questions.q: Isometric scale is constructed using lines at
questions.why: The isometric scale is built using a 45° line (true length) and a 30° line (isometric length) from the same point, which gives the 0.816 ratio.

questions.q: Polar array of 8 holes on a circle: angle between holes
questions.why: The holes are equally spaced around a full turn, so the angle is 360°/8 = 45°.

questions.q: Case: A 60 × 40 × 20 block has a 20 × 20 notch through its top front edge. In isometric drawing, the notch depth along the receding axis is
questions.why: An isometric drawing uses true lengths along the axes, so the 20 mm notch depth is drawn at 20 mm along the 30° axis. Reducing it to 16.3 mm would apply to an isometric projection.
options: drawn at true 20 mm along the 30° axis

questions.q: Relative polar input to draw a 50 mm line at 120°
questions.why: Relative polar entry is @length<angle, so a 50 mm line at 120° is @50<120. The other forms put the numbers in the wrong order or style.

questions.q: Hidden line in CAD should be placed on
questions.why: A hidden line belongs on its own layer with a dashed linetype, so it can be shown, hidden or printed separately.
options: a hidden-line layer with dashed linetype

questions.q: Radius of a sphere in isometric projection drawing
questions.why: A sphere looks like a circle from every direction, so even in isometric projection its outline is drawn at the true radius.

questions.q: Which view arrangement indicates first-angle on a CAD sheet?
questions.why: In first-angle projection the top view is placed below the front view. Third angle puts it above.
options: Top view above the front view
Top view below the front view

quiz.why: In front of VP means the top view, after the planes are opened, lies below XY. It's 20 mm below, the distance from VP.
A line perpendicular to VP is viewed end-on in the front view, so its front view is a point.

quiz.q: Mock 1: Cone parallel to generator section
quiz.why: Cutting a cone with a plane parallel to a generator gives a parabola. Cutting parallel to the axis gives a hyperbola.
Cones are developed by the radial-line method, since their generators all meet at the apex. Parallel-line is for prisms and cylinders.

quiz.q: Mock 1: Angle of isometric receding axes with horizontal
quiz.why: In isometric drawings the receding axes are drawn at 30° to the horizontal.

questions.q: Hidden edges line type
questions.why: Hidden edges are shown as thin dashed lines. Thick lines are for visible edges and chain lines for centre lines.

questions.q: Top view plane
questions.why: The top view is projected on the horizontal plane, HP.

questions.q: Cylinder base Ø20: development width
questions.why: The development of a cylinder's side is a rectangle whose width equals the circumference: π × 20 ≈ 62.8 mm.

questions.q: Isometric axes angle
questions.why: The three isometric axes are 120° apart. 90° would be the usual axes of orthographic views.

questions.q: Diagonal scale RF 1:2500 for 500 m max: length
questions.why: 500 m = 50 000 cm, and with RF 1/2500 the scale length is 50 000/2500 = 20 cm.

questions.q: Ellipse focus 45 mm from directrix, e = 2/3: VF
Line 80 mm parallel to HP, 45° to VP: FV length
questions.why: A line parallel to HP shows its true length in the top view, and its front view is parallel to XY. The front view has length 80 cos 45° ≈ 56.6 mm.

questions.q: Square pyramid axis inclined 40° to HP: base makes with HP
questions.why: For a right pyramid, the base is perpendicular to its axis, so if the axis is 40° to HP, the base is at 90° − 40° = 50° to HP.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Third-angle drawings place the top view above the front view.  Reason (R): In third angle the plane lies between observer and object, so views appear on the observer's side.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: A is true: third-angle puts the top view above the front view. R is true and explains it, because the transparent plane lies between the observer and the object, so each view is projected on the observer's side.

questions.q: Cylinder Ø50 cut at 45° to axis: major axis
questions.why: The major axis of the elliptical section is D/sin θ = 50/sin 45° = 50/0.707 ≈ 70.7 mm.

questions.q: Cone Ø70, h = 120: slant height
questions.why: Slant height L = √(35² + 120²) = √(1225 + 14 400) = √15 625 = 125 mm. Remember to use the radius, 35 mm, not the diameter.

questions.q: Sector angle for that cone
Involute of a 50 mm circle: string length at 1/4 turn
questions.why: After a full turn the string is the circumference πD, so after 1/4 turn it is π × 50/4 ≈ 39.3 mm.

questions.q: Case: A duct is a cylinder Ø100 × 200 mm. Sheet needed for its lateral surface (no overlap)
questions.why: The side surface unrolls to a rectangle: width πD = π × 100 ≈ 314 mm and height 200 mm.

questions.q: TL of a line whose TV is 40 mm and whose ends differ in height by 30 mm
questions.why: The true length is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs 40 and 30: √(1600 + 900) = √2500 = 50 mm.

questions.q: Point 20 below HP and 30 in front of VP lies in
questions.why: Below HP and in front of VP is the fourth quadrant. In front of VP alone gives the first or fourth, and below HP then decides.

questions.q: A hexagonal prism resting on HP with two base sides perpendicular to VP: number of vertical edges visible in FV
questions.why: With two base sides perpendicular to VP, a corner faces the viewer. The vertical edges then line up in three positions: left, middle and right, so three lines are visible.

questions.q: CAD: to draw six equal holes on a pitch circle quickly
questions.why: A polar array repeats an object at equal angles around a centre, which is perfect for six equal holes on a pitch circle (60° apart).

questions.q: Isometric projection of a 120 mm sphere outline
questions.why: A sphere's outline looks like a circle from every direction, so in isometric projection it is drawn at true size, Ø120.

questions.q: Development of a frustum of a cone is
questions.why: A frustum develops to the difference of two sectors, which is an annular sector (a ring-shaped piece).
